chant.name: Golden Chanterelle
chant.description: A golden yellow mushroom with a distinctive funnel shape and fruity aroma
chant.howTo: Look for them in deciduous forests, especially near oak and beech trees

guide.identify: Chanterelles are egg-yolk to golden yellow and grow up to 10 cm across. The cap is a shallow funnel with a wavy edge that curls under. Underneath you won't find real gills, but blunt, forking ridges that run down the stem. You can't lift them off one by one like gills. The stem is solid, and the flesh is firm and white to pale yellow. It smells faintly of apricots. Two look-alikes matter. Jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus) have thin, crowded real gills, grow in clusters from wood or buried roots and are orange right through. The false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca) is a deeper orange, soft, and also has thin, crowded gills.
guide.habitat: Chanterelles live with tree roots. They grow under oak, beech, birch, chestnut, spruce and pine, mostly on acid soil in moss. You often find them on banks and beside paths. They are common across Europe, from the lowlands to the mountains. In North America the golden chanterelle is really several close species. Examples are Cantharellus flavus in the East, C. californicus under live oaks in California and C. cascadensis in the Pacific Northwest.
guide.season: In central and northern Europe they come from late June to October, after warm, soaking rain. In southern Europe the season starts later and lasts longer, into winter in Mediterranean oak woods. In the eastern US they fruit in summer after warm rain. In the West they follow the autumn rains, and in California they run on into winter.
guide.picking: Cut or twist them at the base and brush off the soil on the spot. Leave the small ones to grow. In Germany they are specially protected. There you may pick only small amounts, for your own use. Swiss cantons, Italian regions, parts of France and Spain and US public lands set their own limits or permits. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of them, brush chanterelles clean rather than washing them. They soak up water. Never eat them raw. Cook them well, first in a dry pan until the water has gone, then in butter. They taste mild, fruity and slightly peppery, with a firm bite. They are good with eggs, cream, potatoes, pasta and chicken.
guide.keeps: They keep a few days in the fridge in paper, not plastic. Dried chanterelles turn tough. For longer keeping, fry them in butter and freeze them.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature (UK) and MushroomExpert.com. North American species and look-alikes: University of Florida IFAS Extension. Protection: German Federal Species Protection Ordinance. Season: GBIF records.

mushroom.name: Porcini
mushroom.description: The king bolete: a stout brown-capped mushroom with a pale netted stem and white pores that never bruise blue
mushroom.howTo: Found in coniferous and deciduous forest, often near spruce and beech, from late summer into autumn

guide.identify: This is a stout bolete with a pale to chestnut-brown cap. The cap is smooth and greasy but never velvety. It often has a thin whitish rim. The pores are white when young, then turn yellow and olive. They do not change colour when you press them. The pale stem has a fine white net near the top. The white flesh does not change colour when cut. Pink pores and a dark brown net mean the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus). Red or orange pores mean another bolete that may be toxic. So does flesh that turns blue.
guide.habitat: It grows with spruce, pine, beech, oak, sweet chestnut and birch on acid soil. You find it from the lowlands to the tree line, all across Europe. In North America it grows mainly in the Pacific states. In the southern Rockies the redder Rocky Mountain king is commoner.
guide.season: The main season is August to October. In the mountains it starts in June, and in the south it lasts into November. On the US Pacific coast it comes with the autumn rains. A flush usually comes about two weeks after a soaking rain that follows a warm, dry spell.
guide.picking: Twist it out or cut it at the base. Leave the buttons and the old or maggoty caps. Germany allows only small amounts for your own use. Most Italian regions require a permit. Each US national forest sets its own rules.
guide.kitchen: First make sure you have identified it with certainty. Brush it clean and slice it lengthwise to check for maggots. Fry it, or use it in risotto, pasta and soups. Cook it through. Not everyone tolerates it raw, and old or badly stored ones upset the stomach.
guide.keeps: Keep it cool, in paper rather than plastic, for a day or two. It dries very well in thin slices, and it freezes well too.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Regione Piemonte, First Nature and MushroomExpert. Season: GBIF records. Rules: BArtSchV (Germany) and US Forest Service. Cooking: Regione Piemonte and VIDAL.

morel.name: Morchella
morel.description: A distinctive mushroom with a honeycomb cap that appears in spring
morel.howTo: Look in disturbed areas, burned forests, and near dead trees in spring

guide.identify: The cap is a honeycomb of pits and ridges. It can be yellowish, grey-brown or almost black, and it sits on a pale stem. Cut every morel in half lengthways. A true morel is one single hollow from the cap tip to the stem base. Its cap joins the stem at its lower edge. The deadly false morel (Gyromitra esculenta) has a brain-like, reddish-brown head. Inside, it is chambered or cottony. Cooking does not make it safe. Verpa bohemica has a cap attached only at the very top, like a thimble. Its stem is stuffed with cottony pith.
guide.habitat: Look on the ground in open broadleaf and river woods, old orchards and gardens. Morels often grow by ash, elm, poplar or apple, on lime-rich soil or bark mulch. In the eastern US, look by dying elms, ash and old apple trees. In the western US they come up in conifer forest the spring after a fire.
guide.season: Morels come from March to May. They appear earlier in the lowlands of southern Europe. In the north and in the mountains they come later, into June. They follow soaking spring rain once the soil warms. In the mountains of the western US they follow the melting snow.
guide.picking: Cut the stem at ground level with a knife. Carry morels in a basket or mesh bag. In Germany all morels are protected, and you may take small amounts for your own use only. Elsewhere, many regions and US national forests set limits or ask for a permit. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you have identified them with certainty, cook morels thoroughly. Raw or undercooked morels are toxic, and that includes dried ones. France's food-safety agency ANSES advises 20 to 30 minutes in the pan for wild mushrooms. Large meals have caused dizziness and trembling, even when the morels were cooked. So keep portions modest. They suit butter, cream, asparagus and chicken.
guide.keeps: They keep two days in the fridge, in a paper bag. Morels dry very well. Soak dried morels, then strain the soaking water into the sauce. Cook them as long as fresh ones.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Missouri Department of Conservation and First Nature. Toxicity and cooking: ANSES and Lagrange and Vernoux (Toxins, 2020). Rules: German Federal Species Protection Ordinance and US Forest Service. Season: GBIF records.

blackberry.name: Blackberry
blackberry.description: Sweet, dark purple berries that grow on thorny bushes
blackberry.howTo: Found in hedgerows, woodland edges, and disturbed areas in late summer

guide.identify: Brambles have long, arching stems armed with hooked prickles. Each leaf has three or five toothed leaflets spread like a hand. They are dark green on top and paler underneath. The flowers are white or pink, with five petals. The berries are made of many small round drupelets. They go from green to red to glossy black. A ripe blackberry comes off with its white core inside. A raspberry leaves its core on the plant and is hollow. Rubus fruticosus is a group of hundreds of closely related brambles. You use them all the same way.
guide.habitat: Look in hedgerows, at woodland edges and in clearings, scrub, wasteland and railway banks. It grows on almost any soil, across Europe except the far north. In the US, native blackberries grow in old fields and at woodland edges. The introduced Himalayan blackberry forms dense thickets in the Pacific Northwest and California.
guide.season: In the south of Europe and in the US the berries ripen from July. Further north they start in late July or August. They keep coming until the first frosts in September and October. Flowers, green fruit and ripe fruit often hang on the same bush.
guide.picking: Pick only fully black berries that come away with a gentle pull. Leave the red ones, and leave some for wildlife. Avoid busy roadsides and edges sprayed with weedkiller. In central Europe there is fox tapeworm to think about. Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for it. It still advises washing them well. Only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of the plant, you can eat the berries raw or cooked. Bake them in crumbles and pies with apple, or make jam, jelly, syrup and vinegar. Rinse them just before you use them and check for insects. The flavour ranges from sweet to sharp, from one bush to the next.
guide.keeps: Unwashed and spread out in a shallow box, they keep a day or two in the fridge. To freeze them, spread them on a tray and bag them once they are hard. Frozen berries suit cooking.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and uses: Woodland Trust. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

elderberry.name: Elderberry
elderberry.description: Small dark purple berries that grow in clusters on elder trees
elderberry.howTo: Look for elder trees in hedgerows and woodland edges in autumn

guide.identify: Elder is a shrub or small tree with grey-brown, corky, furrowed bark. The twigs have soft white pith inside. The leaves are opposite, with five to seven toothed leaflets. American elderberry can have up to eleven. In early summer it carries flat heads of creamy, scented flowers. These become broad clusters of small purple-black berries on reddish stalks. When ripe, the clusters droop under their weight. Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus) is a soft herb that dies back each winter. Its berry clusters stand upright above the leaves. Red elder (Sambucus racemosa) has red berries in upright, dome-shaped clusters. Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana) is a tall herb with smooth purple-red stems. Its berries are strung along long spikes, not held in flat clusters.
guide.habitat: Look in hedgerows, at woodland edges, in scrub, on riverbanks, on wasteland and at the edges of villages. It likes rich, moist soil and grows across Europe except the far north. In the eastern US the native American elderberry grows along streams, wet ditches and field edges. In the west you find blue elderberry on open slopes and in valleys. Its ripe berries carry a dusty blue bloom.
guide.season: The berries ripen in early autumn. In warm lowlands they start in late August. Further north and in the mountains they run through September into October. The creamy flower heads come earlier, from late May.
guide.picking: Cut whole clusters with scissors when every berry is purple-black. Leave clusters that still have green or red berries. Avoid busy roadsides, and leave plenty on each bush for the birds.
guide.kitchen: Elderberries must be cooked. Raw or unripe berries, stems, leaves and seeds contain compounds that release cyanide during digestion. They can cause nausea, vomiting and stomach cramps. Thorough cooking breaks them down. Once you've identified them with certainty, strip the berries from the stalks with a fork. Throw away green berries and every bit of stem. Simmer them into syrup, jelly, juice, soup or pie filling. The taste is dark, earthy and tart. It goes well with apple, pear, cinnamon and lemon. Never use red elderberries for food.
guide.keeps: Fresh clusters keep a day or two in the fridge. If you freeze them whole, the berries shake off the stalks easily. Frozen or dried berries must still be cooked before you eat them.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust. Toxicity, cooking and keeping: Oregon State University Extension.

nettle.name: Nettle
nettle.description: A nutritious green plant with stinging hairs that must be cooked
nettle.howTo: Found in disturbed areas, hedgerows, and woodland edges in spring and summer

guide.identify: Nettles grow upright, with square stems and leaves in opposite pairs. The leaves are heart-shaped to oval, coarsely toothed and pointed. Stems and leaves are covered in stinging hairs. From early summer, thin tassels of tiny greenish flowers hang where the leaves join the stem. Dead-nettles look similar, but they don't sting. They also have showy white, yellow or purple lipped flowers.
guide.habitat: Nettles grow in dense patches on rich, moist soil. Look at woodland edges, riverbanks, ditches and hedgerows, and around farms and old buildings. They are common throughout Europe. In the south they keep mostly to damp, shaded places. They also grow across most of the US, especially along streams and in moist open woods.
guide.season: Young shoots appear from February in mild areas and from March further north. You can pick them until the plant flowers, from about June. Patches that have been cut or mown send up fresh shoots. That gives you a second picking in late summer and autumn.
guide.picking: Wear gloves. Snip the top few pairs of leaves with scissors and leave the roots. Avoid roadsides, sprayed field edges and paths where people walk dogs. Nettle patches also feed the caterpillars of many butterflies.
guide.kitchen: Always cook or blanch nettles before you eat them. Heat takes away the sting, and so does drying them well. Drop the washed tops into boiling salted water for a few minutes. Then use them like spinach, in soup, risotto, omelettes or pesto. They taste like spinach, only a little earthier.
guide.keeps: Blanch them, squeeze them and freeze them in portions, and they keep for months. For tea, dry the leaves in a shady, airy place.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and cooking: NC State Extension and Woodland Trust. Season: Woodland Trust and GBIF records.

dandelion.name: Dandelion
dandelion.description: A common weed with bright yellow flowers and edible leaves
dandelion.howTo: Found in meadows, grasslands, and disturbed areas during growing season

guide.identify: Dandelion grows as a rosette at ground level. The leaves are hairless and deeply, raggedly lobed. Their teeth point back towards the centre. Leaves and stalks bleed white milky sap when you break them. Each flower stalk is leafless, unbranched and hollow. It carries one head of yellow, strap-shaped florets. Later comes a round white seed clock. Cat's-ear has branched, solid stalks and hairy leaves. Hawkbits have forked hairs on the leaves. Sow-thistles carry several flowers on leafy stems. Only pick plants that match every point.
guide.habitat: It grows in lawns, meadows, pastures, verges and waste ground, in sun, from the lowlands into the mountains. You find it almost everywhere in Europe. It was brought from Europe to the US and now grows throughout the country.
guide.season: A big flush of flowers comes in early spring, mainly in April and May. In the mild south it comes earlier. After that, flowers appear on and off until autumn. The leaves are least bitter in early spring, before the first buds appear.
guide.picking: Cut young leaves at the base. Pick the flowers on a sunny day when they are fully open, and leave plenty for early bees. Avoid lawns treated with weedkiller, roadsides and places where dogs are walked. Only dig roots where you have the landowner's permission, such as in your own garden.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of the plant, eat young leaves raw in salads. They are pleasantly bitter, as in the French salad with bacon. Boil older leaves for about 10 minutes to take off some bitterness. Then fry them with garlic and oil. Use the flowers cooked. Make fritters, or simmer them with sugar and lemon into a thick syrup. Cleaned roots can be roasted as a coffee substitute. Eaten in quantity, the roots are a laxative. The milky sap can irritate skin. People allergic to the daisy family can react, so try a small amount first.
guide.keeps: The leaves keep a few days in a bag in the fridge. Use the flowers straight after picking, as they close quickly. Roasted roots keep in an airtight jar.
guide.source: Identification: BSBI and NC State Extension. Picking and cooking: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension and Colorado State University Extension. Safety: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

hazelnut.name: Hazelnut
hazelnut.description: Sweet, round nuts that grow on hazel trees
hazelnut.howTo: Look for hazel trees in hedgerows and woodland edges in autumn

guide.identify: Hazel is a shrub or small tree with many stems. Its leaves are round and doubly toothed, pointed at the tip and soft and downy underneath. In late winter yellow catkins hang from the bare twigs. The nuts grow in bunches of one to four. Each sits in a frilly, green, leafy husk that covers about three quarters of it. They turn brown as they ripen. North America's wild hazels are close relatives. The beaked hazelnut's husk forms a long bristly tube.
guide.habitat: It grows in the understorey of woods, in hedgerows and in scrub across Europe. In the south it is mostly found in hills and mountains. It fruits best in sun, at woodland edges. In the US the European hazel grows mainly in orchards in Oregon. The wild species grow in thickets, clearings and at woodland edges.
guide.season: The nuts come from late August to October. They are ready when the husk browns and they fall or come loose with a light shake. Squirrels, jays and dormice often get there first.
guide.picking: Gather fallen nuts or shake the branches lightly. Leave plenty for wildlife. Skip nuts with a small round hole, because a weevil larva has eaten the kernel. Skip light ones too. Avoid busy roadsides and sprayed field edges.
guide.kitchen: Once you're sure of the plant, eat them raw or roast them until the skins crack. Then rub the skins off in a rough cloth. Use them in cakes, pralines, pesto and salads. Hazelnuts are a common cause of nut allergy.
guide.keeps: Dry them in the shell in an airy place until the kernel is cream-coloured right through. Then store them somewhere cool and dry. Dried nuts keep up to a year in the fridge.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. Drying and storage: Oregon State University Extension.

garlic.name: Wild Garlic
garlic.description: A pungent herb with broad leaves and white flowers
garlic.howTo: Found in deciduous woodlands in spring, often forming large patches

guide.identify: Each leaf of wild garlic grows on its own thin stalk straight from the ground. The blade is soft, bright green and a pointed oval, with parallel veins. It is matt underneath. From April a leafless stalk carries a rounded cluster of white, star-shaped flowers. Crush a leaf and wild garlic smells strongly of garlic. Its deadly look-alikes do not. But the smell stays on your fingers, so after the first few leaves the test proves nothing. Check every leaf by its stalk and outline too. Lily of the valley has two or three leaves wrapped around one another at the base. Autumn crocus has tough, stalkless leaves in a tuft. Lords-and-ladies has arrow-shaped leaves with net veins. White false hellebore has pleated leaves along an upright stem. Solomon's seal has leaves alternating along an arching stem.
guide.habitat: It forms carpets in damp, shady deciduous woods. It grows especially in beech woods and floodplain woods on rich soil, and along shaded streams. It is common in central and northern Europe, including Britain. In southern Europe you find it mostly in mountain woods.
guide.season: The leaves come up from February in mild places, and in March and April elsewhere. They are best before the flowers open. It flowers from April to June, later in the mountains. By early summer the leaves are gone.
guide.picking: Pick leaf by leaf, never by the handful. That way no look-alike growing in the same patch ends up in your basket. Leave the bulbs in the ground. Britain bans digging up wild plants without the landowner's permission. Germany allows only a small amount for your own use. Many nature reserves ban picking, so check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of it, use the leaves raw or add them at the end of cooking. Put them in pesto, soups, risotto and butter, or have them with eggs. The flowers go on salads. Wash each leaf under running water. In central Europe the authorities advise this because of fox tapeworm. Its eggs survive freezing but not cooking.
guide.keeps: The leaves keep two or three days in the fridge in a damp cloth. Chopped leaves and pesto freeze well. Keep anything in oil in the fridge and use it within a few days.
guide.source: Identification and look-alikes: Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES), German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) and Woodland Trust. Season: Woodland Trust and GBIF records.

chickenOfTheWoods.name: Chicken of the Woods
chickenOfTheWoods.description: A bright orange-yellow bracket fungus that grows on trees
chickenOfTheWoods.howTo: Look for it growing on dead or dying trees, especially oaks

guide.identify: Chicken of the woods grows as overlapping, fan-shaped brackets 10 to 40 cm wide, with no stem. Young ones are soft, moist and bright yellow to orange. With age they fade to cream and turn chalky. The underside is sulphur-yellow with tiny pores, not gills. The flesh is white to pale yellow and does not change colour when cut. An orange cluster on wood with gills underneath is the poisonous jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus). In the western US, the closely related Laetiporus gilbertsonii and Laetiporus conifericola look much the same.
guide.habitat: This fungus rots wood. It grows on living and dead broadleaf trees, most often oak. You also see it on sweet chestnut, cherry, willow and beech, and now and then on yew. It is common in lowland Europe and the eastern US, in woods, parks and streets. In the western US its relatives grow on oaks, eucalyptus and conifers.
guide.season: It appears from late spring to autumn, mostly in summer, a few days after warm rain. In the western US it comes mainly in autumn. The same tree often fruits for several years.
guide.picking: Cut the soft edges of young brackets with a knife. Leave the tough base and the old, chalky brackets. Never pick it from yew, which is highly poisonous. Don't pick it from trees along busy roads either. Where mushroom picking needs a permit or has daily limits, check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: When you're certain what it is, cook it thoroughly. Raw or undercooked, it upsets the stomach. Even well cooked, it disagrees with some people, causing nausea, dizziness and vomiting. So try a small amount first. Slice it and fry or braise it. The firm flesh is often compared to chicken. It goes well with lemon, garlic and herbs.
guide.keeps: It keeps a few days in the fridge in a paper bag. It freezes well, raw or cooked.
guide.source: Identification and hosts: Woodland Trust, First Nature and MushroomExpert.com. Western species: Bay Area Mycological Society. Reactions: University of Florida IFAS Extension.

oysterMushroom.name: Oyster Mushroom
oysterMushroom.description: A white-grey mushroom with fan-shaped cap that grows in clusters on dead wood
oysterMushroom.howTo: Look for them growing on dead trees, especially beech and oak, in autumn and winter

guide.identify: Oyster mushrooms have a shell- or fan-shaped cap, 5 to 18 cm across. It can be blue-grey, grey-brown or cream. They grow on wood in overlapping tiers. The white to cream gills run down into a short, off-centre stem, or there is no stem at all. The flesh is white and firm, and the smell is mild. The spore print is white to pale lilac. Three look-alikes matter. The poisonous jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus) is bright orange, gills included. It grows in tufts at the foot of trees. Sulphur tuft (Hypholoma fasciculare) has sulphur-yellow caps on central stems. Its gills are greenish-yellow and turn purple-brown, and it tastes bitter. Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens) have been linked to deaths in Japan. They are pure white, thin and translucent, and grow only on rotting conifer wood.
guide.habitat: It grows on dead or dying broadleaf trees, mainly beech. You also find it on poplar, willow, oak and ash, and rarely on conifers. Look on standing trunks, stumps and fallen logs. It is common across Europe and North America.
guide.season: This is a mushroom of late autumn and winter. A cold spell or the first frosts after rain set it off. In southern Europe it goes on into January or February. In the eastern US it fruits from October to early April.
guide.picking: Cut the cluster at the base with a knife. Take firm young caps and leave old or beetle-riddled ones. Some places need a permit for mushroom picking or set daily limits, so check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Be certain of the identification before you cook it. Cook it well and don't eat it raw. Trim the tough base and tear the caps into strips. Fry them hot until the edges crisp. The taste is mild and slightly sweet. It goes with garlic, butter, soy sauce and eggs.
guide.keeps: It spoils fast. Keep it in a paper bag in the fridge for a few days, or cook it and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and season: First Nature and MushroomExpert.com. Angel wings: Beaty Biodiversity Museum, University of British Columbia.

shiitake.name: Shiitake
shiitake.description: A mushroom with brown cap and white gills, highly prized in Asian cuisine
shiitake.howTo: Found growing on dead hardwood trees, especially oak and beech, in spring and autumn

guide.identify: The cap is brown to dark reddish-brown and flattens with age. It often has whitish flecks near the edge, and it cracks in dry weather. The gills are white to cream and bruise brown. The stem is tough, fibrous and often off-centre. The spore print is white. The deadly funeral bell (Galerina marginata) also grows on logs. It is smaller and honey-brown, with a ring on the stem and a rusty-brown spore print.
guide.habitat: Shiitake is native to East Asia, where it grows on dead broadleaf wood such as oak and Castanopsis. In Europe and North America it is grown on oak logs or sawdust blocks. It has been found outside cultivation only a few times, for example in the Netherlands. So a brown mushroom on a fallen log in the woods is almost certainly something else.
guide.season: Logs kept outdoors fruit in spring and autumn. A flush comes a few days after soaking rain in mild weather. Growers also force a flush by soaking a log in cold water.
guide.picking: Pick the caps while the edge is still curled under. Twist them off or cut the stem at the log. Pick only from logs you grow or have permission to pick from.
guide.kitchen: Make sure of the identification, then cook it thoroughly. Raw or lightly cooked shiitake can cause shiitake dermatitis. That is an itchy rash of whip-like streaks, about a day later. The stems are too tough to eat, but they flavour stock. Fry or simmer the caps with soy sauce, ginger and garlic. They have a deep, savoury taste.
guide.keeps: It keeps a few days in the fridge in a paper bag. It dries very well. Soak dried caps before use and keep the water as stock.
guide.source: Origin and distribution: Naturalis Biodiversity Center. Log growing: Cornell Cooperative Extension. Shiitake dermatitis: DermNet.

raspberry.name: Wild Raspberry
raspberry.description: Sweet red berries that grow on thorny canes with distinctive compound leaves
raspberry.howTo: Look for raspberry canes in hedgerows, woodland edges, and disturbed areas in summer

guide.identify: Raspberries grow on upright canes, often head-high. The canes are covered in small, fine prickles, not the hooked thorns of a blackberry. Each leaf has three to seven toothed leaflets set along a stalk. They are green above and white-felted beneath. The small white flowers hang downwards. When you pick a red berry, its white core stays on the plant. So a picked raspberry is a hollow cap.
guide.habitat: Look in woodland clearings and edges, on felled and burnt ground and on rocky slopes. It also grows in scrub, heathland and hedgerows, from the lowlands into the mountains across Europe. It moves into new clearings and fades as the trees grow back. In the US, American red raspberry grows across the north and in the western mountains. The black raspberry, with purple-black hollow berries, grows in the east.
guide.season: Raspberries ripen in summer. In southern Europe and the lowlands they start in June. In the north and in the mountains they ripen in July and August. Up high they sometimes last into September.
guide.picking: Pick berries that are fully red and slip off the core without pulling. Put them in a shallow container, as they crush easily. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm. It still advises washing them well. Only heating above 60 °C kills the tapeworm's eggs. Home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: With the identification certain, eat them raw or use them for jam, syrup, cakes and desserts. Wild raspberries are smaller and more aromatic than garden ones. Rinse them briefly just before use. Check them for the small white larvae of the raspberry beetle.
guide.keeps: Raspberries are very perishable. Eat them the same day, or keep them unwashed in the fridge for a day or two. To freeze them, spread them on a tray first, then bag them. Frozen berries suit sauces and baking.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

blueberry.name: Wild Blueberry
blueberry.description: Small sweet blue berries that grow on low shrubs in acidic soil
blueberry.howTo: Found in heaths, moors, and acidic forests in summer and early autumn

guide.identify: Bilberry, also called whortleberry, is a low deciduous shrub, usually below knee height. Its stems are green and angled. The leaves are small and oval, with finely toothed edges. In spring, pinkish flowers shaped like lanterns hang one by one. Each gives one blue-black berry with a pale bloom. At the tip of the berry sits a small ring shaped like a crown. The flesh is purple-red right through. Cultivated blueberries have pale flesh. Its poisonous look-alikes are soft herbs, not woody dwarf shrubs. Deadly nightshade (Atropa bella-donna) is tall, and its shiny black berries sit in a green star of five sepals. Herb Paris (Paris quadrifolia) carries one berry on top of a stem with a whorl of four leaves. Solomon's seal (Polygonatum) hangs blue-black berries beneath an arching, unbranched stem.
guide.habitat: It needs acid, nutrient-poor soil. Look in conifer, birch and oak woods and on heaths and moorland, from the lowlands to above the treeline. It is common across northern and central Europe and in the mountains of the south. You won't find it on lime. In North America it grows wild in the western mountains. In the east, the wild blueberries people pick are lowbush and highbush blueberries (Vaccinium angustifolium, Vaccinium corymbosum). These are close relatives with pale flesh.
guide.season: In the lowlands the berries ripen from July. In the mountains and the north the season runs through August into September. A late frost at flowering can cut the crop.
guide.picking: Pick by hand. Berry combs strip leaves and damage the plants. Some places ban them or set daily limits, such as the Vosges in France and Tuscany in Italy, so check the local rules. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm. It still advises washing them well. Only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: When you're sure of the plant, eat them raw or put them in tarts, pancakes, jam and compote. They are sweet and sharp. They also stain fingers, teeth and clothes. Rinse them briefly just before use, and pick out leaves and green berries.
guide.keeps: Unwashed and spread out, they keep a few days in the fridge. Freeze them on a tray, then bag them. They also dry well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust; look-alikes: Yle (Finnish public broadcaster). Picking rules: Vosges prefecture and Region of Tuscany. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

strawberry.name: Wild Strawberry
strawberry.description: Small red berries with intense flavor, with white flowers and trifoliate leaves
strawberry.howTo: Look for them in meadows, woodland edges, and grassy areas in spring and summer

guide.identify: Wild strawberry is a low plant. Its long-stalked leaves have three toothed leaflets, bright green and slightly glossy. It spreads by runners that root along the ground. The end tooth of each leaflet is as long as its neighbours, or longer. The flowers are white, with five rounded petals and a yellow centre. The fruit is a small red cone with tiny seeds on the surface, hanging from a thin stalk. Barren strawberry (Potentilla sterilis) flowers earlier. It has gaps between its notched petals and an end tooth shorter than its neighbours. It has no fleshy fruit. Mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) has yellow flowers and round, spongy, tasteless berries.
guide.habitat: Look at woodland edges and in clearings, on sunny banks and path sides, at hedgerow bases and in old grassland. It often grows on dry, stony or lime-rich soil, from the lowlands into the mountains across Europe. In the US it grows in open woods and clearings in the north and in the western mountains. The larger Virginia strawberry (Fragaria virginiana) is the usual wild strawberry of fields and meadows there.
guide.season: It flowers from April. In southern Europe the berries ripen from late May, and elsewhere from June. The plants keep fruiting through the summer. In the mountains and the north they go on into August.
guide.picking: Pick only fully red berries by pinching the stalk. Never pull up the plants. In England wild strawberry is listed as near threatened, so pick sparingly there. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm. It still advises washing them well. Only heating above 60 °C kills the tapeworm's eggs. Home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: With the plant identified with certainty, eat the berries raw and soon. Rinse them briefly just before eating. Their flavour is more intense than that of garden strawberries, but it varies from plant to plant. A handful is enough to scent cream, yoghurt or a tart.
guide.keeps: They spoil quickly in a warm basket. Keep them cool and eat them the same day. You can freeze them, but they thaw soft.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland (BSBI). Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

wildMint.name: Wild mints
wildMint.description: Any wild mint: water mint, horse mint, apple mint, corn mint and pennyroyal. Square stems, opposite leaves and a mint scent when crushed
wildMint.howTo: Found in damp ground, ditches and along streams. Pennyroyal is fine as a light tea (poleo menta) but toxic as an oil or in quantity: avoid it in pregnancy

guide.identify: All mints have square stems and leaves in opposite pairs. A crushed leaf has a clear mint smell. Small lilac, pink or white flowers grow in whorls, or in heads and spikes at the shoot tips. Water mint has hairy, oval leaves and a rounded flower head. Horse mint has long, grey-hairy leaves. Apple mint has round, wrinkled, soft leaves. Corn mint flowers only in whorls along the stem. Pennyroyal is small and creeping, with tiny leaves and a sharp smell. Unscented square-stemmed plants such as gipsywort grow among them. The smell also stays on your fingers. So smell each stem on its own, and leave any that does not smell of mint.
guide.habitat: Most wild mints like wet ground. Look at stream and pond edges, in ditches, marshes and wet meadows. Corn mint also grows in damp fields. Pennyroyal grows in grassland that floods in winter, mostly in southern and western Europe. In the US the native American wild mint grows in wet places across most of the country. Spearmint, peppermint and pennyroyal have escaped from gardens there.
guide.season: Shoots appear in spring and are most tender before flowering. Most mints flower from midsummer into autumn. In southern Europe growth starts earlier.
guide.picking: Pinch off the top few pairs of leaves above a leaf joint and leave the roots. Pick stem by stem, not by the handful. Deadly hemlock water-dropwort and water hemlock grow in the same wet places. Avoid water below farms or sewage outlets.
guide.kitchen: Once you've identified it with certainty, use the leaves for tea. They also go into salads, yoghurt sauces and dishes with peas, potatoes and lamb. Mint from streams, ditches or grazed wet pasture can carry liver fluke, like wild watercress. Use that mint only in hot tea or cooked. Pennyroyal contains pulegone, which harms the liver. A light tea is traditional in Spain and Portugal. But never use the oil, and never drink it strong or often. Never give it to babies, children or anyone pregnant, breastfeeding or with liver disease.
guide.keeps: Hang bunches in a dark, airy place and they dry well for tea. Chopped leaves freeze in ice cubes.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland, The Wildlife Trusts and Native Plant Trust (Go Botany). Pennyroyal: European Medicines Agency and National Capital Poison Center. Liver fluke: Pan American Health Organization. Season: GBIF records.

chickweed.name: Chickweed
chickweed.description: A low-growing plant with small white flowers and oval leaves, very nutritious
chickweed.howTo: Common in gardens, disturbed areas, and meadows during growing season

guide.identify: Chickweed is a low, sprawling plant with weak, round, juicy stems. The leaves are small, pointed ovals in opposite pairs. The lower ones sit on short stalks. A single line of fine hairs runs down the stem. It switches sides at each pair of leaves. The white flowers are star-shaped, with five petals. Each petal is split so deeply that they look like ten. There are two toxic look-alikes. Scarlet pimpernel has square, hairless stems and stalkless leaves with black dots underneath. Its flowers are orange-red or blue. Spurges ooze white, milky sap from a broken stem. Chickweed never does.
guide.habitat: Look in gardens, vegetable beds, field edges and farmyards. It likes disturbed, rich, moist soil, often in light shade. It is one of the commonest plants in Europe and is found across the US.
guide.season: It grows best in cool, damp weather. In the north that means spring and autumn. In mild areas such as southern Europe and the southern US it grows from autumn to spring. Summer heat and drought make it die back until the autumn rains.
guide.picking: Snip or pinch off the leafy top few centimetres. The plant grows back. Only pick where no weedkiller has been sprayed. Stay away from roads and from spots where dogs and cats go.
guide.kitchen: Once you're sure of it, you can eat the leaves, stems and flowers raw or briefly cooked. They taste mild and fresh, a little like young peas. Add them to salads, sandwiches and pesto, or stir them into soups at the end. Wash them well.
guide.keeps: Chickweed wilts quickly. Keep it in a bag in the fridge and eat it within a day or two.
guide.source: Identification: UC Statewide IPM Program and Woodland Trust. Scarlet pimpernel: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture. Season: Woodland Trust and GBIF records.

plantain.name: Common Plantain
plantain.description: A low-growing plant with broad oval leaves and tall flower spikes
plantain.howTo: Found in lawns, meadows, and disturbed areas during growing season

guide.identify: Common plantain grows as a flat rosette of broad, oval leaves on short, wide stalks. Each leaf has three to seven strong veins. They run side by side from base to tip. Snap a leaf stalk and they pull out as tough strings. From early summer, leafless stalks carry long, narrow rat-tail spikes of tiny greenish flowers. Later these fill with small brown seeds. Foxglove is deadly, and its first-year rosette is the one to watch for. It has soft, hairy, wrinkled leaves with a net of veins and no strings. Foxglove leaves have been sold by mistake as plantain.
guide.habitat: Look on lawns, paths, farm tracks, field edges, meadows and gardens. It grows wherever the ground is trampled and compacted. It is native to Europe and Asia and common all over Europe. It is also common across the whole of the US, where it came with European settlers.
guide.season: New leaves appear from early spring to autumn. They are most tender in spring and after mowing. Flower spikes rise from early summer, and the seeds ripen into autumn.
guide.picking: Pick young leaves from the centre of the rosette, a few from each plant. Leave the root in the ground. Avoid roadsides and paths used by dogs. Also avoid lawns or verges that may have been sprayed with weedkiller.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain it's plantain, you can put young leaves raw into salads. Older leaves are tough and stringy. Blanch them or cook them like spinach, and pull out the strings. The taste is mild, grassy and slightly bitter. NC State Extension notes that very large amounts can lower blood pressure. So eat it as one green among others.
guide.keeps: The leaves wilt fast. Keep them in a bag in the fridge for a day or two, or dry them in the shade for tea.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: NC State Extension, Michigan State University Extension and UC IPM. Foxglove mix-up: US FDA (1997). Kitchen: NC State Extension.

walnut.name: Walnut
walnut.description: Large round nuts with hard shells and rich, oily flavor
walnut.howTo: Look for walnut trees in parks, gardens, and woodland edges in autumn

guide.identify: The walnut is a large tree. Its bark is smooth and olive-brown, turning grey and fissured with age. The leaves have five to nine smooth-edged oval leaflets. Crushed, they smell of polish. The nut sits in a thick, smooth green husk that darkens and splits when ripe. The black walnut of the eastern US has more leaflets, and they are narrower and toothed. Its round husk does not split. Inside is a very hard, ridged shell.
guide.habitat: Walnut is native from south-east Europe to south-west China. It has been planted across Europe and gone wild in hedgerows, field edges, riverbanks and young woods. It grows mostly at low altitude on deep, fertile soil. In the US, orchards are mainly in California. In the eastern woods the wild species is the black walnut.
guide.season: Walnuts come in September and October, when the husks crack and the nuts drop. Green walnuts for pickling or liqueur are picked in late June or early July. At that stage a skewer still goes straight through them.
guide.picking: Gather fallen nuts every day or two, before mould and insects spoil them. Wear gloves, because the husk stains skin brown for days. Remove the husks soon. Most walnut trees belong to someone, so ask first.
guide.kitchen: Once you are sure of the tree, eat fresh walnuts with the bitter skin peeled off. Or dry them for bread, cakes, salads and sauces. Throw away mouldy, shrivelled or rancid kernels. Walnuts are a common cause of nut allergy.
guide.keeps: Dry them in the shell in an airy, shady place, until the divider between the halves snaps. Dried nuts keep up to a year in the fridge.
guide.source: Identification and range: Woodland Trust. Harvest and storage: Oregon State University and Kansas State University extension.

chestnut.name: Chestnut
chestnut.description: Large sweet nuts encased in spiny green husks that split open when ripe
chestnut.howTo: Found in chestnut groves and mixed forests in autumn, often near paths

guide.identify: Sweet chestnut leaves are long, narrow and glossy, 16 to 28 cm long. They have sharp saw teeth and many straight, parallel veins. The husk is covered all over in long, fine spines as sharp as needles. It usually holds two or three nuts. They are flattened on one or both sides and end in a small point with a tuft. Don't confuse it with the toxic horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) of parks and streets. That tree has hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets. Its thick green husk has only a few short spikes. Inside are one or two round, glossy conkers with no point. In North America the buckeyes (other Aesculus) are toxic too. A tree with hand-shaped leaves is never a sweet chestnut.
guide.habitat: It is native to southern Europe, western Asia and North Africa and has long been planted for its nuts. It grows on acid, well-drained soil and avoids limestone. Large chestnut woods cover hills from northern Portugal and Galicia to the Cévennes, Corsica and the Apennines. In the US most chestnuts are planted. Blight nearly wiped out the native species.
guide.season: The nuts fall from late September to early November, mostly in October. They come earlier in the lowlands than in the mountains.
guide.picking: Go every few days and gather the nuts that have fallen on their own. Wear thick gloves, or roll the husks open under your boot. Leave nuts with small holes, which come from weevil or moth larvae. Many chestnut woods are private, and the nuts on the ground belong to the owner. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you are sure they are sweet chestnuts, cook them. Raw, they are astringent and hard to digest. Throw away any that float in water. Cut a slit in the shell so they don't burst. Then roast them, or simmer them for about 30 minutes. Peel off the shell and the bitter inner skin while they are warm. They are sweet and floury and go into soups, stuffings and purées.
guide.keeps: At room temperature fresh chestnuts go mouldy within about two weeks. In the fridge they keep about two months. You can also freeze or dry them.
guide.source: Identification: Woodland Trust, ANSES and Oregon State University Extension. Harvest, cooking and storage: Oregon State University Extension.

elderflower.name: Elderflower
elderflower.description: Creamy white flowers that grow in large flat clusters on elder trees
elderflower.howTo: Look for elder trees in hedgerows and woodland edges in late spring and early summer

guide.identify: Elder is a woody shrub or small tree with corky, furrowed, grey-brown bark. Its leaves are opposite, with 5 to 7 toothed leaflets. They smell unpleasant when you crush them. In late spring it carries flat, branching heads of tiny creamy white flowers. These have pale yellow anthers and a sweet, musky scent. Danewort, or dwarf elder, is a soft herb that dies back each winter. It has upright heads and purple anthers. Red elder flowers earlier, in egg- or dome-shaped clusters. Both are toxic. Hemlock, water hemlock and giant hogweed are soft green herbs, not woody shrubs. Giant hogweed's sap burns skin in sunlight. Hemlock has a smooth, hollow, purple-blotched stem and a mousy smell. In all three, the flower stalks spread from one point like the spokes of an umbrella.
guide.habitat: It grows in hedgerows, at woodland edges, in scrub, on riverbanks and on waste ground. It is often near houses, on rich soil. It is common across Europe, from the lowlands into the hills. In the US, the native American elder in the East and blue elder in the West grow in similar places.
guide.season: In northern and central Europe elder flowers from late May into June. In the warm south it starts earlier. In the eastern US, American elder flowers later and over a longer spell, mostly in June and July.
guide.picking: Pick on a dry, sunny morning. Choose heads that are fully open, creamy and sweet-smelling, and pass over browning ones. Cut or snap them at the base. Take only a few from each bush so it can still bear berries. Shake out insects gently.
guide.kitchen: When you're certain it's elder, use only the flowers. Strip them from the stalks, because stalks, leaves, bark, roots and unripe berries are poisonous. Steep the flowers in hot sugar syrup with lemon to make cordial. You can also dip whole heads in batter and fry them as fritters. Don't eat the thick stalk. Or dry the flowers for tea. The taste is sweet and floral, good with gooseberries and strawberries. The berries that follow in autumn must be cooked.
guide.keeps: The flowers fade fast, so use them the day you pick them. Heads dried in the shade keep for tea in an airtight jar. Cordial keeps a few weeks in the fridge, or you can freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and BSBI. Look-alikes: University of Minnesota Extension. Picking and cooking: Penn State Extension and UMass Extension.

daisy.name: Common Daisy
daisy.description: Small white flowers with yellow centers that grow close to the ground
daisy.howTo: Common in lawns, meadows, and grassy areas during spring and summer

guide.identify: The common daisy is a low plant. Its spoon-shaped, slightly hairy leaves form a flat rosette pressed to the ground. Each leafless, hairy stalk carries one flower head about 2 cm across. It has white rays, often tipped with pink, around a yellow centre. The heads close at night and in dull weather. Some plants look similar but are different. Oxeye daisy and other bigger daisy-like flowers grow on leafy stems. Mayweeds and chamomiles have feathery leaves.
guide.habitat: It grows in lawns, short turf, grazed pastures, verges and paths, in sun on moist soil. You find it almost everywhere in Europe. It came to the US from Europe. There it now grows in lawns and damp, disturbed ground, most of all where summers are cool.
guide.season: Where winters are mild it flowers almost all year. The main flush comes from spring into early summer. In cold regions and much of the US it flowers from spring to early summer. After that you see scattered flowers until frost.
guide.picking: Pinch off flower heads and a few young leaves. Take from many plants and leave the rosettes in place. Avoid lawns treated with weedkiller or fertiliser, places where dogs are walked and roadsides.
guide.kitchen: Once you've identified it with certainty, you can eat the flowers and young leaves raw in small amounts. Use them in salads and sandwiches or as a garnish. They taste mild to slightly bitter, and older leaves are tough. Rinse them gently in cool water. Try only a little at first. People allergic to the daisy family can react, and large amounts can upset the stomach. Avoid it in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.
guide.keeps: Pick them just before use, as the flowers wilt quickly. Until then, keep them between damp paper towels in the fridge.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: The Wildlife Trusts and NC State Extension. Cooking and safety: Colorado State University Extension and NC State Extension.

violets.name: Sweet Violet
violets.description: Small purple flowers with heart-shaped leaves and a sweet fragrance
violets.howTo: Found in woodland edges, hedgerows, and shady areas in early spring

guide.identify: Sweet violet is a low plant with a rosette of long-stalked leaves. They are heart-shaped with a rounded base, scalloped edges and short hairs. It spreads by long runners that root. Each flower rises on its own stalk from the rosette. It has five uneven petals, and the lowest has a short spur at the back. The flowers are usually deep violet, sometimes white, with blunt sepals and a sweet scent. Dog violets look similar but have no scent. Lesser celandine is poisonous and grows in the same places. It has glossy, fleshy, hairless leaves and flowers with 8 to 12 shiny yellow petals. Lords-and-ladies is poisonous too. It has glossy, arrow-shaped leaves with lobes pointing backwards.
guide.habitat: Look at woodland edges, on hedge banks and in shady grass, churchyards, parks and old gardens. It likes moist, rich soil in part shade. It grows across most of Europe and has escaped from gardens in many places. In the US it grows wild locally, in lawns and woodland edges.
guide.season: It flowers from February to May, earlier in the mild south. In much of the US it flowers in April and May. A few flowers sometimes appear again in late summer. The leaves are best young, in spring.
guide.picking: Pick a few flowers and young leaves from each patch. Leave the rosette and roots in the ground, and never dig up plants. Avoid sprayed lawns, verges and places where dogs are walked.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of the identification, you can put the flowers raw on salads and desserts. You can also candy them with pasteurised egg white and fine sugar. Or steep them in boiling water and sweeten it for violet syrup. Young leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked like spinach. They are mild and slightly thicken soups. Never eat the roots or seeds, which can cause vomiting. Try a small amount first.
guide.keeps: The flowers wilt fast. Keep them between damp paper towels in the fridge and use them the same day. Candied flowers keep in an airtight container in a cool, dark place.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: NatureSpot and NC State Extension. Cooking: Colorado State University Extension and NC State Extension.

amaranth.name: Amaranth
amaranth.description: A leafy green plant, often considered a weed, with edible leaves and seeds rich in nutrients.
amaranth.howTo: Look for it in disturbed soils, gardens, and fields during summer. Young leaves are best harvested before flowering.

guide.identify: Redroot amaranth, or pigweed, is a stout, upright annual. Its stem is covered in fine white hairs and is red at the base. The taproot is pink to red. The leaves grow alternately and are oval to diamond-shaped, smooth-edged and long-stalked. They often have a small notch or a tiny point at the tip. The tiny green flowers sit in dense, bristly, prickly spikes. Later these hold tiny, shiny black seeds. Two toxic weeds share its ground. Thorn apple (Datura) has large, coarsely toothed leaves that smell foul, white trumpet flowers and spiny pods. Black nightshade has wavy-edged leaves, small white star flowers and black berries.
guide.habitat: Look in gardens, fields and farmyards and on waste ground. It wants bare, rich, disturbed soil in full sun. It is native to central and eastern North America. Today it is a common weed across the US and much of Europe, most of all in warm lowlands.
guide.season: This is a summer annual. It comes up in late spring once the soil warms. It flowers from about July to September. The seed ripens from August to October, until the first frost. The leaves are best young, before the plant flowers.
guide.picking: Pick the young leaves and tender tops by hand before flowering. Once the seeds are black, rub them out of the seed heads. Stay away from roadsides and sprayed fields. Skip heavily manured or fertilised ground and drought-stressed plants. Those build up the most nitrate.
guide.kitchen: Make sure of your identification first. Then cook the leaves like spinach. Boil them briefly and pour the water away, which lowers their nitrate and oxalate. Eat them in moderation. Don't eat them at all if you have kidney stones or kidney disease. They taste mild and earthy and go well with garlic, beans and eggs. You can toast the seeds or cook them like a grain.
guide.keeps: The leaves wilt within a day. Keep them in a bag in the fridge, or blanch and freeze them. Dry the seed heads in a paper bag. Then rub out the seeds, winnow them and store them in a closed jar.
guide.source: Identification and season: Cornell University and NC State Extension. Nitrates and oxalates: NC State Extension and Michigan State University Extension. Thorn apple mix-ups: Marseille poison control centre.

artichoke.name: Wild Artichoke
artichoke.description: A thistle-like plant with edible flower buds and stems, related to the cultivated artichoke.
artichoke.howTo: Found in meadows and fields, harvest young flower buds and tender stems in spring and early summer.

guide.identify: Wild artichoke, also called wild cardoon, forms a large rosette of deeply cut leaves. They are silvery grey-green on top and almost white underneath, felted with hairs. Each lobe ends in a stiff yellow spine. In late spring a stiff, branched stem grows up to head height. It carries heads like small artichokes, wrapped in spine-tipped bracts. These open into blue-purple thistle flowers. Watch out for Atractylis gummifera, a deadly Mediterranean thistle. People have mistaken it for wild artichoke, and it has killed people in Morocco. It has no stem. Its pink flower head sits flat in the middle of the spiny rosette. It flowers in late summer and autumn, and its root oozes a sticky gum. Never eat a stemless thistle rosette or a thistle root.
guide.habitat: It likes dry, sunny, open ground. You find it in pastures, at field edges, on roadsides, on fallow land and in scrub, often on clay. It is native to the Mediterranean, from Portugal to Greece and North Africa. In northern and central Europe it is only a garden escape. In California it is an invasive weed of grassland and coastal scrub below 500 m. Elsewhere in the US it is a garden plant.
guide.season: The rosette grows after the autumn rains and right through the mild winter. You pick the leaf stalks from late winter to spring. The heads come in late spring and early summer. It flowers mainly in June and July. Then it dries off in the summer drought.
guide.picking: Wear thick gloves and cut the stalks or heads with a knife. Leave the root in the ground. In its native range, leave some heads to flower. California is different, because there it is invasive. Take heads before they seed and never move seed heads around. Check local rules on public land.
guide.kitchen: Be certain of your identification before you start. Peel the spines and strings off the leaf stalks. Drop the pieces into lemon water straight away, because they blacken. Boil them until tender. They taste like a bitter artichoke, and people stew them or fry them in batter. From the heads, strip off the spiny bracts and eat the tender base and heart. The dried flowers curdle milk for cheeses such as Serra da Estrela and Torta del Casar.
guide.keeps: The stalks keep a few days in the fridge, wrapped in a damp cloth. Once boiled, they freeze well.
guide.source: Identification, range and season: IUCN Global Invasive Species Database and California Invasive Plant Council. Atractylis poisonings: Moroccan poison control data.

asparagus.name: Wild Asparagus
asparagus.description: A perennial plant with slender, edible shoots that appear in spring.
asparagus.howTo: Look for young shoots in open fields, meadows, and along hedgerows in spring.

guide.identify: Wild asparagus is a tangled, evergreen, woody shrub up to about 1.5 m tall. It has no true leaves. Instead it has tufts of short, stiff, needle-like green branchlets, each ending in a sharp spine. Its black berries are not eaten. In spring, thin shoots push up from the base of the old spiny bush. They are dark green to purplish and often thinner than a pencil. Small pointed scales lie pressed to the stem, and there are no leaves. Black bryony and white bryony are poisonous climbers of the same hedges, and they also sprout in spring. Black bryony soon unfolds glossy heart-shaped leaves. White bryony is hairy, with lobed leaves and tendrils. Only pick shoots that rise from an asparagus bush you can see.
guide.habitat: It grows in Mediterranean scrub, at the edges of holm oak and pine woods, in olive groves and hedges and along stone walls and roadsides. You find it from the coast into the hills of Portugal, Spain, southern France, Italy, the Balkans and Greece. It does not grow wild in northern and central Europe. Asparagus there is garden asparagus gone wild, mostly on sandy ground.
guide.season: The shoots come up from late winter to spring, after the autumn and winter rains. On warm coasts they start in February. In the hills they run into April and May. Rain followed by mild, sunny days brings a new flush.
guide.picking: Snap each shoot by hand where it breaks easily. Leave some on every bush, and never cut or uproot the bush. In Italy each region sets its own rules. Tuscany, for example, allows picking only until 31 May. In Spain the landowner and the regional government decide, and parks often ban picking. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: When you're sure what you have, use only the tender part above where the shoot snaps. It is more bitter than garden asparagus. Cook it briefly. It is good in omelettes and scrambled eggs, risotto or pasta, or sautéed with garlic and olive oil.
guide.keeps: It is best eaten the same day. It keeps a few days in the fridge standing in a little water. You can also blanch and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Mediterranean floras and the University of the Balearic Islands virtual herbarium. Bryonies: RHS. Picking rules: Regione Toscana.

black_chant.name: Black Trumpet (Horn of Plenty)
black_chant.description: A dark, funnel-shaped mushroom with a rich, smoky flavor, prized in gourmet cooking.
black_chant.howTo: Found in deciduous forests, especially under oak and beech, in late summer and autumn.

guide.identify: You're looking for a thin, hollow horn 4 to 8 cm across. It is open right down to the base and has no separate cap. The inside is grey-brown to black and finely scaly. The outside is ash-grey and smooth or only faintly wrinkled, with no gills or ridges. As it ripens it turns paler, with a whitish bloom. The flesh is thin, brittle and grey-black, with a faint, sweet smell. Black trumpets of the eastern US (Craterellus fallax) look the same. They give a pinkish-orange spore print rather than a white one. The ash-grey chanterelle (Craterellus cinereus) has clear forked ridges on the outside.
guide.habitat: It lives with broadleaf trees, mainly beech and oak, and also hornbeam and hazel. Look in damp leaf litter and moss, on rich, loamy soil, in gullies and on banks. It often grows in large groups. It is common across Europe. In the eastern US its counterpart grows under oak and beech. On the Pacific coast a western black trumpet grows under tanoak, live oak and madrone.
guide.season: It is mainly an autumn mushroom. In Europe it runs from late summer to November, into December in mild years and later still around the Mediterranean. In the eastern US it comes from July to October, after heavy rain. On the Pacific coast the western black trumpet fruits from midwinter into spring.
guide.picking: Pinch or cut it at the base. Leave the small ones and take only what you will eat. Local limits on wild mushrooms apply. It hides well in dark litter, so where you find one, look closely around it.
guide.kitchen: Be sure of what you've found before it goes in the pan. Split each trumpet lengthwise and rinse out leaves, insects and grit. Then drain it well. Never eat it raw. Cook it well, in butter, cream sauces, risotto or pasta, or with fish and eggs. The taste is deep and smoky, and it gets stronger after drying.
guide.keeps: Fresh, it lasts only a few days in the fridge. It dries quickly and very well. Keep it in a closed jar, or grind it to a powder for sauces and soups.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature (UK), MushroomExpert.com and MykoWeb (California Fungi). Season: GBIF records.

lingonb.name: Lingonberry
lingonb.description: Small, red, tart berries that grow on low evergreen shrubs in acidic soils.
lingonb.howTo: Look for them in coniferous forests, moorlands, and heathlands in late summer and autumn.

guide.identify: Lingonberry, also called cowberry, is a creeping evergreen dwarf shrub. Its leaves are thick, glossy and dark green, with edges that roll under. The pale underside is speckled with tiny dark dots. Small white to pink bell-shaped flowers grow in short clusters at the shoot tips. They give round, glossy red berries that hang in small bunches. Bearberry (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi) is a trailing shrub of the same places. It has net-veined leaves without dots and dry, mealy berries. The poisonous red and black berries do not grow on a low evergreen carpet. Yew (Taxus) is a tree or tall shrub with flat needles. Its red cup is open at the end around a dark seed. Mezereon (Daphne mezereum) is an upright shrub with berries pressed along the stem. Deadly nightshade (Atropa bella-donna) is a tall herb with black berries. Red baneberry (Actaea) and lily of the valley (Convallaria majalis) are soft herbs.
guide.habitat: It needs acid, poor soil. Look in pine and spruce forests, birch woods, heaths and moorland and on mountain slopes above the treeline. It is very common in Scandinavia and the Baltic states and is found in the Alps and other mountains. In North America it grows mainly in Canada and Alaska. It reaches the US only in the far north, from Minnesota to Maine. There it is rare, and in Wisconsin it is endangered.
guide.season: The berries turn red from August. They are best when fully dark red, from September into October. They hang on the plants into winter.
guide.picking: Pick dark red berries by hand, or with a berry picker where that is allowed. In Sweden, Finland and Norway, everyman's right lets anyone pick wild berries away from houses and gardens. Nature reserves can have their own rules, though. In central Europe, Bavaria's health authority (LGL) says eating wild berries has not been shown to be a risk factor for fox tapeworm. It still advises washing them well. Only heating above 60 °C kills its eggs, and home freezing does not.
guide.kitchen: Raw berries are sour and slightly bitter. So once you've identified them with certainty, you usually cook them with sugar into a sauce or jam. In Sweden people also stir them raw with sugar. Serve them with meatballs, game, roasts, potato pancakes or porridge.
guide.keeps: They keep longer in the fridge than most berries. Stirred with sugar, they keep cool for a long time thanks to their natural benzoic acid. They freeze well as they are.
guide.source: Identification and range: Minnesota Wildflowers and CREA Mont-Blanc. Picking rights: Swedish Environmental Protection Agency. Fox tapeworm: Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL).

masterwort.name: Masterwort
masterwort.description: A perennial herb with aromatic leaves and white flower clusters, used in traditional medicine and as a spice.
masterwort.howTo: Found in mountain meadows and forest clearings, harvest leaves and roots in spring and summer.

guide.identify: Masterwort is a hairless umbellifer 30 to 100 cm tall. Its stem is round, grooved and hollow. The leaves split into three, and then into three again. They end in broad, oval, double-toothed leaflets 5 to 10 cm long. The upper leaves sit on large, inflated sheaths. The umbels are flat and white or pinkish, with up to 50 rays. The fruits are round, flat and broadly winged. A crushed leaf or the thick brown rootstock smells strongly spicy, of celery and carrot. Its deadly look-alikes have finely divided leaves, feathery or like a fern's. Hemlock has a smooth, purple-blotched stem and a mousy smell. Fool's parsley has long bracts hanging under each small umbel. Cowbane (water hemlock) has a rootstock split into hollow chambers when you cut it lengthways. Hemlock water dropwort has pale tubers in wet ground. Giant hogweed is far bigger, with a bristly, purple-blotched stem. Its sap burns skin in sunlight. Masterwort's own sap can also make skin sensitive to sunlight.
guide.habitat: It grows in damp mountain meadows and tall-herb stands, on stream banks and scree and in alder scrub. Mostly you find it between 1,400 and 2,700 m. It grows in the Alps, the Pyrenees, the Carpathians and other mountains of central and southern Europe. In Germany it is native only in the Bavarian Alps. Lower down it is rare and usually escaped from old gardens, as in Britain and Scandinavia.
guide.season: The leaves grow as the snow melts. They are best young, in early summer. It flowers from late June to August, and the fruits ripen in September and October.
guide.picking: Wear gloves. Take a few leaves from a large stand and leave the rootstock in the ground. Digging the root often needs a permit. In Tyrol that comes from the district authority. Many reserves and national parks ban picking. It grows among monkshood and white false hellebore, and both are deadly. Pick leaf by leaf, and only from a plant you have identified as a whole.
guide.kitchen: Be certain of your identification first. Use it as a seasoning, not a vegetable, because it is strongly bitter and spicy, like lovage. In the Alps the root flavours schnapps (Meisterwurzbrand) and herb cheese. Chop a few young leaves finely and add them sparingly to soups and fresh cheese. Wash your hands after handling it.
guide.keeps: Dry the leaves or slices of root in an airy, shaded place. Then store them in a closed jar.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland and Alpine floras. Root digging and schnapps: Austrian Ministry of Agriculture (register of traditional foods). Skin reactions: Botanical Dermatology Database.

parasol.name: Parasol Mushroom
parasol.description: A large, tall mushroom with a broad, scaly cap resembling a parasol, edible when young.
parasol.howTo: Look for it in meadows, grasslands, and forest edges from late summer to autumn.

guide.identify: The parasol is a tall mushroom. Its cap starts as a closed, egg-shaped drumstick. It opens into a flat umbrella 10 to 25 cm across. The cap is cream with brown scales and a smooth brown bump in the centre. The gills are white, free and crowded. The slender stem grows up to 30 cm tall and has a bulb at the base. It has a brown snakeskin pattern and a thick double ring that slides up and down. The spore print is white. Several look-alikes matter. The deadly Lepiota species are small, with caps of only a few centimetres. Chlorophyllum molybdites gives a greenish spore print. The shaggy parasols (Chlorophyllum rhacodes and C. brunneum) upset many people. They have a smooth stem, and their flesh turns orange-red when cut. Amanita pantherina has white warts on the cap and a ring that does not slide. It also has a rimmed bulb at the base.
guide.habitat: It grows in grassland and at woodland edges. Look in pastures, meadows, clearings, rides and dunes. It likes well-drained soil, from the lowlands to the mountains. It is common across Europe.
guide.season: Parasols come in summer and autumn, mainly from July to October. In southern Europe they go on into November. They come up after a spell of warm, wet weather.
guide.picking: Pick only open, full-size caps where you can check every feature. Lift the whole mushroom so you can see the base. Leave any parasol-like mushroom with a cap under 10 cm. Leave old, tough ones too. Check the local rules, because many regions limit how much you may pick.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of it, eat only the cap, and cook it. Like most wild mushrooms, it can upset the stomach raw. Bread it and fry it like a schnitzel, or grill it with butter and garlic. It tastes mild and nutty. You can dry the tough stems and grind them for soups.
guide.keeps: It keeps two days in the fridge. Sliced caps dry well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature. Look-alikes and poisonings: ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

sorrel.name: Common Sorrel
sorrel.description: A tangy, lemon-flavored leafy plant often used in salads and soups.
sorrel.howTo: Harvest young leaves in meadows, grasslands, and along paths in spring and summer.

guide.identify: Sorrel has tender, arrow-shaped leaves. Their two pointed basal lobes point backwards, down the stalk. The upper leaves clasp the stem. Where each leaf joins the stem, a thin, papery sheath wraps around it. From May the flowering stems carry loose spikes of small reddish flowers. Lords-and-ladies (Arum maculatum) is toxic, and its young leaves have a similar shape. But they often carry dark spots and have rounded lobes. They grow in woods and hedges rather than open grassland. Never taste a leaf to check it, because lords-and-ladies burns the mouth.
guide.habitat: Look in meadows, pastures, lawns, verges and open woods, from the lowlands into the mountains. It is very common throughout Europe. In the US it is introduced and scattered. You find it mainly in the north-east, around the Great Lakes, in Oregon and in Alaska. There the smaller sheep's sorrel is far more common.
guide.season: Leaves grow from early spring, and in mild places almost all year. They are best young. Once the plant flowers, from May, they turn tougher and more bitter. Cut plants send up new ones, though.
guide.picking: Pick single young leaves from each plant and leave the root. Choose meadows that are not sprayed or fertilised, away from roads and dog paths.
guide.kitchen: Be certain of the identification first. The leaves are sharply sour, like lemon peel. Shred young ones into salads, or cook them briefly into soups, omelettes and sauces for fish and eggs. The sourness comes from oxalic acid. Eat sorrel in moderation, and avoid it if you have kidney stones. Cook it in stainless steel or enamel, not aluminium or cast iron.
guide.keeps: The leaves wilt within two or three days in the fridge. Cooked down to a purée, sorrel freezes well.
guide.source: Identification and look-alikes: Woodland Trust and Wild Food UK. US range: Flora of North America. Oxalic acid: Wild Food UK. Season: GBIF records.

st_george.name: St. George's Mushroom
st_george.description: A white, firm mushroom with a mealy scent, appearing around St. George's Day in spring.
st_george.howTo: Found in grassy areas, meadows, and along woodland edges in spring.

guide.identify: St George's mushroom is stout and fleshy, white to cream. The cap is 5 to 15 cm across, often lumpy, with an inrolled edge. The gills are white, narrow and very crowded. The thick, solid stem has no ring and no sac at the base. The firm white flesh does not change colour. It smells strongly of fresh meal. The spore print is white. The deadly Inosperma erubescens has a pointed, streaky cap. It reddens where handled and gives a brown spore print. Entoloma sinuatum can smell mealy too. But its gills turn pink and its spore print is pink. White Amanitas such as the deadly Amanita verna are also out in spring. They have a ring and a sac at the base.
guide.habitat: It grows in grass, in pastures, mown verges, parks and woodland edges. You often find it by hawthorn, blackthorn and other hedgerow shrubs, mostly on lime-rich ground. It comes back to the same spots for years, often in rings. It grows across Europe and is much sought after in northern Spain and central Italy.
guide.season: It comes in spring, mainly in April and May. In the north and in the mountains it lasts into June. It is named after St George's Day, 23 April. A mild, wet spring brings it on.
guide.picking: Cut the stem at the base and leave the small ones. Take young, firm caps, as older ones are often full of maggots. Avoid busy verges. Check the local rules too, because some regions require a permit or set a daily limit.
guide.kitchen: Once you're sure of it, eat it cooked. Cooking takes away most of the mealy smell. The firm, mild flesh suits omelettes, scrambled eggs, risotto and cream sauces. Cut each one lengthways first to check for maggots.
guide.keeps: It keeps up to two days in the fridge, wrapped in paper. It freezes well after a quick sauté.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature. Look-alikes: First Nature and ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

truffle_b.name: Black Truffle
truffle_b.description: A highly prized underground fungus with a strong aroma, used in gourmet cuisine.
truffle_b.howTo: Found underground near the roots of oaks and hazelnuts, typically harvested with trained animals in winter.

guide.identify: This truffle is a round, lumpy tuber that grows underground. It ranges from walnut to fist size. The black skin is reddish when young and covered in small, hard, many-sided warts. Cut it in half. Ripe flesh is purplish-black, marbled with fine white veins that turn reddish-brown in the air. It smells strong and earthy. Earthballs (Scleroderma) are poisonous. They have a thick, yellowish to brown, scaly skin and smell of gas. Inside they are firm and dark. The winter truffle (Tuber brumale) and the imported Chinese truffle (Tuber indicum) look similar. But they are worth far less.
guide.habitat: It grows underground among the roots of oaks, above all holm and downy oak, and of hazel. It needs well-drained, lime-rich soil in sunny hill country. A patch of bare, burnt-looking ground around a tree often shows where it grows. It is native to southern France, eastern Spain and central Italy. Much of the crop now comes from planted truffle orchards.
guide.season: It ripens in winter, from December to March. Markets peak in January. Storms in late July and August, while it swells, decide the size of the crop.
guide.picking: You find it with a trained dog. Dig only where the dog marks, with a small truffle spade. Take only ripe truffles and fill the hole again. Truffle hunting is regulated. Italy requires a licence after an exam, and its regions set the seasons. Spanish regions set seasons and permits. In France truffles belong to the landowner. In Germany wild truffles are protected. Check the local rules before you look.
guide.kitchen: If you're certain of the identification, brush it clean under cold water just before use. Shave or grate it raw over warm dishes. Or warm it gently in fat, with eggs, butter, pasta, risotto or potatoes. Long cooking kills the aroma.
guide.keeps: Wrap it in kitchen paper in a closed jar in the fridge. Change the paper daily and use it within days, as the aroma fades. Eggs kept in the jar take on its scent. Freezing keeps the aroma better than drying.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: CRPF Languedoc-Roussillon and Trufamania. Rules: Italian truffle law 752/1985, Spanish regional rules and German Federal Species Protection Ordinance. Season: GBIF records.

bronze_bolete.name: Bronze Bolete
bronze_bolete.description: A dark bronze to almost black-capped porcino with a pale netted stem and firm white flesh
bronze_bolete.howTo: Look on warm lowland slopes under oak and sweet chestnut, later in the season than the summer bolete

guide.identify: This is the darkest porcino. The cap is dark chestnut to almost black, often with bronze patches. It stays dry and finely velvety, even when wet. The pores are white, then yellow to olive, and they don't turn blue. The pale brown stem has a fine brown net, densest at the top. The very firm white flesh does not change colour when you cut it. The summer bolete is paler, and its net runs further down the stem. Two other boletes share its oak woods. These are the devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) and Le Gal's bolete (Rubroboletus legaliae). Both have red pores and flesh that turns blue.
