guide.habitat: It likes warm, sunny slopes with oak, sweet chestnut and beech, mostly between 200 and 1,000 m. It is common around the Mediterranean. In Italy you find it along the Apennines and on the islands. It is rare in Britain and Germany.
guide.season: It can appear from July after summer storms. Its main season is September and October, later than the summer bolete. In the south it runs into November. It fruits when a soaking rain and cooling soil follow a hot spell.
guide.picking: Cut it or twist it out, and leave the young ones to grow. In Germany it is rare and specially protected, so don't pick it there. Italy and Spain have regional permits and daily limits.
guide.kitchen: This is the firmest of the porcini. It has a nutty taste that gets stronger when dried. Once you've identified it with certainty, treat it like porcini. Brush it, check for maggots and cook it through.
guide.keeps: It dries and freezes very well in slices.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Regione Piemonte and First Nature; GBIF records. Protection: BArtSchV (Germany). Cooking: Regione Piemonte.

pine_bolete.name: Pine Bolete
pine_bolete.description: A red-brown capped porcino of pine woods, with a stout reddish netted stem and firm flesh
pine_bolete.howTo: Look in mossy pine and spruce forest on acidic sandy soil, in a late spring flush and again in autumn

guide.identify: This is the red porcino. The cap is wine-red to mahogany and often bumpy. It is velvety when young and greasy to slimy when wet, with a whitish bloom at the edge. The stem is short and stout, flushed reddish brown, with a fine whitish to reddish net. The flesh is white, but wine-red just under the cap skin. The pores go from white to yellow and olive. They barely change colour when you press them. The bronze bolete is sepia to black, with no red. Red or orange pores (Rubroboletus satanas) rule it out. So do pink pores with a dark net (Tylopilus felleus).
guide.habitat: It grows mostly with Scots pine and spruce on acid ground, often in moss. In the mountains it also grows with chestnut, beech and fir, mainly at 400 to 1,400 m. It is common in Scandinavia, in Scotland's pinewoods and in the mountains of central and southern Europe.
guide.season: It is often the first porcino of the year and the last. A first flush comes in May and June where it stays cool and moist. The main crop follows in September and October. It goes on into November, past the first frosts.
guide.picking: Cut or twist it out, and don't rake the moss, which shelters the fungus. Many Italian and Spanish regions require a permit. Some Swiss cantons limit amounts. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: If you've identified it with certainty, cook it through like porcini. It is milder and slightly resinous. Very firm young ones need longer cooking. It tints the cooking water green. It suits sauces, pickling and drying.
guide.keeps: It dries well in slices. Fresh, use it within a day or two.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Regione Piemonte and First Nature; GBIF records. Cooking: Regione Piemonte.

summer_bolete.name: Summer Bolete
summer_bolete.description: The earliest porcino, with a finely cracked pale brown cap and a stem netted from top to bottom
summer_bolete.howTo: Look under oak and beech from late spring, well before the other porcini appear

guide.identify: The summer porcino has a matt, dry, velvety cap, pale hazel to mid-brown. In dry weather the cap cracks into a fine network. It is never greasy, and its edge is no paler than the centre. Its clearest mark is a raised net that runs down the stem almost to the base. The pores are white, then yellow-olive, and do not change colour. The white flesh is softer than in porcini. The devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) and Le Gal's bolete (Rubroboletus legaliae) share its oak woods. But they have red pores and flesh that turns blue. The bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus) has pink pores and a dark net.
guide.habitat: It grows with oak and sweet chestnut, and also with beech, lime and birch. Look at wood edges, in parks and on sunny slopes, from the lowlands to about 1,000 m. It is common in central and southern Europe, especially in south-west France and Portugal. In Britain it is rare.
guide.season: This is the first porcino of the year. It starts in May on low ground and in June in the mountains. The main season is July to early September, after warm rain. It lasts until the first autumn cold.
guide.picking: Cut or twist it out and leave the small ones. In hot weather many are maggoty. Halve them on the spot and leave infested ones in the wood. Many Italian and Spanish regions require a permit.
guide.kitchen: Many cooks rate it the finest porcino. It is sweet, nutty and fragrant, and good for drying, sauces and egg dishes. Once you've identified it with certainty, cut away maggoty parts and cook it through.
guide.keeps: Of all the porcini, it keeps worst. Cook or dry it the day you pick it.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and season: Regione Piemonte and First Nature; GBIF records. Cooking: Regione Piemonte.

pacific_chant.name: Pacific Chanterelle
pacific_chant.description: A large golden chanterelle of the Pacific Northwest, paler and pinker than its European cousin
pacific_chant.howTo: Look in mossy Douglas fir and hemlock forest once the autumn rains have set in

guide.identify: This is a large chanterelle, paler and pinker than the European one. The cap is orange-yellow to apricot. Young caps often have fine brownish scales and a pinkish cast, which can vanish in wet weather. Underneath are blunt, forking ridges that run down the stem. They are pale orange-yellow and usually tinged pink. The stem tapers downward, and the flesh is whitish and firm. The cap bruises yellowish. Jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus) and the false chanterelle have thin, crowded true gills. The scaly vase chanterelle (Turbinellus floccosus) is a deep, hollow, orange-red trumpet with coarse scales. It upsets many people's stomachs.
guide.habitat: It lives with conifers, mainly Douglas fir and western hemlock, and also Sitka spruce. Look in moss and needle litter, in second-growth and old forest. It grows mostly in the lowlands and foothills. Its range runs from British Columbia through Washington and Oregon to northern California. In Oregon it is the state mushroom.
guide.season: You find it from September to December, sometimes into January. It needs the autumn rains to soak the ground first, so a dry autumn delays it. Each mushroom grows slowly. In cool, wet weather it can keep growing for weeks.
guide.picking: Cut it at the base and leave the small buttons to grow on. Take only what you will eat. Rules differ by national forest, state and park. Some require a free permit and set daily limits. Many state parks forbid picking. Selling needs a commercial permit. Check with the land manager.
guide.kitchen: When you're certain what it is, brush off the needles and soil. Rinse it only if it's gritty, then dry it, because rain-soaked ones hold water. Never eat it raw. Dry-fry it first to drive off the water, then finish it in butter. It is mild, fruity and firm. It's good with eggs, cream, pasta, salmon and game.
guide.keeps: It keeps several days in the fridge in a paper bag. Dried, it turns tough. To keep it longer, fry it in butter and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification: MushroomExpert.com and UBC Beaty Biodiversity Museum. Picking rules: US Forest Service. Season: GBIF records.

smooth_chant.name: Smooth Chanterelle
smooth_chant.description: An orange chanterelle whose underside is nearly smooth instead of ridged, with a strong apricot smell
smooth_chant.howTo: Look in southeastern oak woods through the humid summer, often in troops on bare soil

guide.identify: The smooth chanterelle is bright orange-yellow to egg-yolk yellow and 2.5 to 8 cm across. It starts flat and later becomes a shallow vase with a wavy edge. Its underside sets it apart. It is smooth or only shallowly wrinkled, with no true gills. It is paler than the cap, often pinkish, and runs down the stem. The stem tapers to the base. The flesh is white and does not change when cut. The smell is usually strong and sweet, like apricots. Jack-o'-lanterns (Omphalotus illudens) are common in the same oak woods. They have sharp, crowded true gills and grow in tight clusters from wood or buried roots. They are also orange inside.
guide.habitat: It lives with oaks and sometimes hickories. Look in hardwood and oak-pine woods across the eastern US, east of the Rocky Mountains. It is most common in the Southeast. It often comes up in troops on bare or mossy soil along paths, stream banks and road cuts.
guide.season: This is a summer chanterelle, from June to September and most often from July. It comes soon after warm, heavy rain in humid weather.
guide.picking: Cut it at the base, leave the small ones and take only what you will eat. Rules differ by state, park and national forest. Many state parks forbid picking, so check before you go.
guide.kitchen: Be sure of the identification, then brush off the soil. The smooth underside holds little grit. Never eat it raw. Cook it well, slowly in butter or in a cream sauce. It is fruity and mild like other chanterelles. It's good with eggs, grits, pasta, chicken and pork.
guide.keeps: A paper bag in the fridge keeps it for a few days. Drying makes it tough. For longer keeping, fry it in butter and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: MushroomExpert.com and University of Florida IFAS Extension. Season: GBIF records.

winter_chant.name: Winter Chanterelle
winter_chant.description: A small brown-capped chanterelle on a hollow yellow stem, fruiting on through the first frosts
winter_chant.howTo: Look in mossy conifer litter late in the season, often in dense troops on rotting wood

guide.identify: The winter chanterelle is small and slim. The cap is 1 to 4 cm, brown to yellow-brown. It is a thin funnel, and its centre opens into the hollow stem. Underneath are blunt, forking ridges, grey to yellowish-grey, that run down the stem. The stem is yellow to orange-yellow, hollow and often flattened or grooved. The deadly webcap (Cortinarius rubellus) grows in the same mossy conifer woods. It has a pointed red-brown cap and true rusty-brown gills. Its stem is solid, with faint yellow bands. It destroys the kidneys. Check every mushroom as you pick and again as you clean. Norway's poison centre advises throwing away the whole basket if you find even one webcap in it.
guide.habitat: It grows on wet, acid ground in conifer woods, mainly under spruce and pine. Look in moss, at bog edges and on moss-covered rotten logs. It is common in northern and central Europe and in the mountains of the south. In North America it grows in the Pacific Northwest and northern California. It also grows in the northern and eastern conifer forests.
guide.season: It comes late in the year. In Europe it fruits from September until hard frost, often still in November and December. On the US Pacific coast it runs from autumn through winter. It needs a wet autumn, and light frosts do not stop it.
guide.picking: Cut the stems above the moss to keep the basket clean. Leave the smallest ones. Keep to local limits, such as small amounts for your own use in Germany. In southern Bavaria and the Bavarian Forest it still carries caesium from Chernobyl. There, eat it only now and then.
guide.kitchen: Make sure of the identification first. Then split the hollow stems and rinse out needles and grit. Never eat it raw. Cook it well, in butter, sauces or soups, or with game. It tastes earthy and stronger than its size suggests.
guide.keeps: It keeps a few days in the fridge in paper. It dries very well and keeps its flavour for months in a closed jar. You can also cook it and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification: MykoWeb (California Fungi) and First Nature (UK). Deadly webcap: Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS). Season: GBIF records.

eastern_king.name: Eastern King Bolete
eastern_king.description: The king boletes of eastern oak woods: a tan to lilac-brown cap, white pores that turn yellow with age and a netted stem, never bruising blue
eastern_king.howTo: Look under oak, beech and hickory in eastern hardwood forest from June, a few days after warm summer rain

guide.identify: This is a small group of eastern king boletes. Boletus variipes has a dry, velvety cap, tan to grey-brown, that often cracks. Boletus separans has a lilac-brown to liver-red cap that fades to yellow-brown. It also shows lilac on the stem. Both have white pores when young that turn yellowish. Both have a clear white to brownish net on the stem. Their white flesh does not change colour. Bitter Tylopilus have pores that turn pink. One example is the violet-grey Tylopilus plumbeoviolaceus. Red or orange pores (Neoboletus subvelutipes) mean a toxic bolete. So do bluing pores and flesh (Boletus sensibilis, Boletus huronensis).
guide.habitat: It grows with oaks, and also with beech and other hardwoods, east of the Rockies. It is most common from New York and the Great Lakes through Pennsylvania and the Appalachians to Georgia and the Ozarks. Boletus nobilis and Boletus atkinsonii belong to the same group.
guide.season: It fruits from June to September, most of all in July and August. Look after warm, soaking summer rain.
guide.picking: Cut it or twist it out and slice it on the spot. Summer kings are often maggoty. Some national forests need a free permit and set daily limits. Parks have their own rules, which are often stricter.
guide.kitchen: Make sure of your identification, then cook it through like porcini. Sauté it, or add it to pasta, soups and stews. You can also dry it for a deeper flavour. Use only firm, fresh ones.
guide.keeps: It dries very well in thin slices. Fresh, use it within a day or two.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: MushroomExpert (Michael Kuo). Season: GBIF and iNaturalist records. Rules: US Forest Service.

rocky_king.name: Rocky Mountain King
rocky_king.description: A stout high-mountain porcino with a brick-red to red-brown cap, white pores and a thick pale stem netted at the top
rocky_king.howTo: Look under spruce and fir high in the southern Rockies once the summer monsoon rains arrive, from July to September

guide.identify: This is a big, stout porcino of the high Rockies. The cap is brick-red to reddish-brown and tacky when fresh. Young caps often have a whitish bloom. It is redder than the porcini (Boletus edulis) that also grow there. The pores are white and stuffed when young, then turn yellow and olive. They do not bruise. The thick, pale stem has a fine white net, at least near the top. The white flesh does not turn blue. Aspen boletes (Leccinum) have dark scales on the stem. Orange-capped ones have caused severe stomach poisonings in Colorado. Red or orange pores mean a toxic bolete.
guide.habitat: It grows mainly with Engelmann spruce, and also with fir and Douglas fir. You find it from about 2,400 m up to the tree line. It grows in Colorado, New Mexico and the mountains of Arizona.
guide.season: It fruits from July to September, sometimes into October. It starts with the monsoon storms and moves upslope through the season. In dry summers it barely fruits.
guide.picking: Twist it out gently, since much of the stem is underground. Leave very maggoty ones. Each national forest sets its own rules. Some ask for a free permit and set daily limits.
guide.kitchen: Be certain of the identification first. On mature caps, remove the yellow, soft pores. They can taste bitter and turn slimy. Then cook it through like porcini, or dry it.
guide.keeps: Dry it in thin slices, or sauté it and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Arora and Frank (2014), MushroomExpert and Forage Colorado. Season: GBIF records. Rules: US Forest Service.

lions_mane.name: Lion's Mane
lions_mane.description: A white, shaggy clump of long hanging spines on hardwood trees that cooks up like crab
lions_mane.howTo: Look on wounded or dead oak, beech and maple from late summer into autumn, often high on the trunk. In Europe it is rare and protected in places, so leave it there

guide.identify: Lion's mane is a single white, rounded clump 8 to 24 cm across. It has no cap or gills. Soft spines 1 to 5 cm long hang from it like icicles. It turns yellow with age. The flesh is white and soft and does not change colour when cut. The spore print is white. Its relatives coral tooth (Hericium coralloides) and bear's head (Hericium americanum) are branched and have shorter spines.
guide.habitat: It grows from wounds in living broadleaf trees and on dead trunks. Most often that is oak, but also beech and maple, and often high up. You find it across the US, more in the East. In Europe it is rare, on old beech and oak in ancient woods.
guide.season: Look from late summer to late autumn, after rain. In warm areas such as California it carries on through winter. It often returns to the same tree.
guide.picking: In Europe, leave it. It is rare and protected by law in several countries, including the UK, Poland, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia and Sweden. Photograph it and report the find. In the US, cut fresh white clumps at the base with a knife. National forests and parks may need a permit or ban collecting, so check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of it, cook it. Slice it and dry-fry it to drive off the water. Then brown it in butter. The mild, sweet taste and stringy texture are often compared to crab. Yellowed clumps taste sour.
guide.keeps: It keeps a few days in the fridge in a paper bag. Freeze it after cooking.
guide.source: Identification and season: MushroomExpert.com and Wild Food UK. Protection: IUCN Red List and the UK Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

hen_of_the_woods.name: Hen of the Woods
hen_of_the_woods.description: A big rosette of overlapping grey-brown fronds at the foot of old oaks, with white pores underneath
hen_of_the_woods.howTo: Look at the base of old or dying oaks from late August to October; it often comes back to the same tree year after year. It is protected in parts of central and northern Europe

guide.identify: Hen of the woods forms a rosette 15 to 40 cm across. It is made of many overlapping grey-brown caps, shaped like spoons or fans and each 3 to 14 cm wide. They branch from a shared white base. The underside is white with tiny pores, not gills. The flesh is white and firm and does not stain when cut or bruised. The black-staining polypore (Meripilus) has larger, thicker caps that bruise black. The umbrella polypore (Polyporus umbellatus) has round caps on small central stems.
guide.habitat: Look at the base of old oaks. Sometimes it grows on stumps or on other broadleaf trees. It rots the roots and comes back to the same tree for years. It is common in the eastern US and rare in the West. In Europe it is uncommon and declining, found under old oaks and sweet chestnuts.
guide.season: It fruits from late summer to late autumn, mostly in September and October. It often appears after the first cool nights that follow rain.
guide.picking: Cut the rosette at the base with a knife. Take only fresh, firm ones, and leave the tree to fruit again. In Europe it is protected by law in Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. It is red-listed in Germany, Austria and elsewhere. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once it's identified with certainty, cook it thoroughly. Shake and rinse soil and insects from between the caps, and trim the tough core. Fry or roast it. The caps crisp at the edges and taste rich, earthy and slightly peppery.
guide.keeps: It keeps several days in the fridge in a paper bag. It freezes well after cooking, and it dries well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: MushroomExpert.com. Status in Europe: IUCN Red List.

saffron_milk_cap.name: Saffron Milk Cap
saffron_milk_cap.description: An orange cap with darker rings that bleeds carrot-orange milk and bruises green; a favourite in Spain and Italy
saffron_milk_cap.howTo: Look under pines and spruces from late summer to November, into winter on the Mediterranean and US Pacific coasts. Break a gill: the milk must be orange to red, never white

guide.identify: The cap is orange with darker concentric rings. When young, its edge is rolled under. Later it turns funnel-shaped and is often blotched green. The crowded orange gills run slightly down the stem. The stem is short, hollow and orange, often with darker orange pits. Break a gill and look at the milk. It is carrot-orange and may slowly turn wine-red. Gills and flesh bruise green. White or yellowing milk means another milk cap. One is the woolly milk cap (Lactarius torminosus). It is pinker, has a woolly, bearded cap edge and grows with birch.
guide.habitat: It grows under pines, on sandy or lime-rich soil. Look in young plantations and grassy clearings, where it often turns up. Close relatives grow under spruce (Lactarius deterrimus) and fir (Lactarius salmonicolor). It is common across Europe, above all in the pine woods of Spain, Portugal and Italy. In North America several related orange-milked species grow under conifers.
guide.season: This is an autumn mushroom. In central and northern Europe it comes from late summer to November. In Mediterranean pine woods it follows the autumn rains, from October into January. On the US Pacific coast it fruits through the wet winter.
guide.picking: Cut the stem at the base and check it for larvae. Leave the small ones. In many regions of Spain and Italy you need a permit or must keep to a daily limit. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: After you've identified it with certainty, cook it well. Grill it with garlic, olive oil and parsley, or stew it with potatoes or rice. It also goes with meat. The flesh is firm and slightly grainy, with a mild, resinous taste. Slow cooking removes any bitterness. The green stains are harmless. Its pigment can turn your urine red, which is harmless too.
guide.keeps: It keeps two days in the fridge. It does not dry well. Cook and freeze it instead, or preserve it in oil or vinegar.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature. Storage: ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

hedgehog_mushroom.name: Hedgehog Mushroom
hedgehog_mushroom.description: A buff to orange cap with soft spines instead of gills underneath: one of the safest wild mushrooms to learn
hedgehog_mushroom.howTo: Look in mossy conifer and broadleaf woods from late summer to late autumn, often in rings or rows; on the US Pacific coast through the winter. Turn it over: spines, not gills

guide.identify: Turn it over. Under the cap you'll find soft, brittle spines 2 to 6 mm long, hanging like small icicles. There are no gills or ridges. The spines rub off easily. The cap is 4 to 15 cm across and cream to buff or pale orange. It is dry, velvety and often lumpy. The stem is white, solid and often off-centre. The firm white flesh slowly bruises yellowish to orange-brown. The terracotta hedgehog (Hydnum rufescens) is smaller and more orange. It has the same soft spines, and so do the American Hydnum species. Other tooth fungi, such as Hydnellum and Sarcodon, are tough and corky or brown and scaly. Many of them are bitter.
guide.habitat: It lives with conifers and broadleaf trees alike, such as spruce, pine, beech, oak and birch. Look in moss and leaf litter. It often grows in rings or rows. It is common across Europe, from the lowlands to the mountains, and across North America. On the US Pacific coast several Hydnum species grow under Douglas fir, tanoak and other trees.
guide.season: In central and northern Europe it comes from late summer to late autumn, often until hard frost. In southern Europe the season is later and longer, running into winter. On the US Pacific coast it arrives with the autumn rains and carries on through the winter.
guide.picking: Cut it at the base. Brush off debris on the spot so it doesn't get stuck in the spines. Leave the small ones. In southern Bavaria and the Bavarian Forest it still carries caesium from Chernobyl. Eat it there only now and then.
guide.kitchen: First be certain of your identification. Brush the cap. On large ones, rub off the spines. They break off in the pan and can taste bitter. Never eat it raw. Cook it well, fried in butter or braised. It tastes mild, nutty and sweet and has a firm, meaty bite. It is good with eggs, potatoes and game and in sauces.
guide.keeps: Because it is firm, it keeps better than most wild mushrooms. It lasts several days in the fridge in paper. For longer keeping, cook it and freeze it.
guide.source: Identification: First Nature (UK) and MykoWeb (California Fungi). Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS). Season: GBIF records.

shaggy_mane.name: Shaggy Mane
shaggy_mane.description: A tall white cylinder of shaggy scales on lawns and roadsides that dissolves into black ink within a day of picking
shaggy_mane.howTo: Look on lawns, verges and disturbed ground a few days after autumn rain, and after spring rain too. Pick only young, all-white ones and cook them the same day; avoid busy roads, where it takes up heavy metals

guide.identify: The shaggy mane is a tall white cylinder, 5 to 15 cm high. It is covered in shaggy, upturned scales, with a pale brown top. With age it opens into a bell. The crowded gills turn from white to pink to black. Then they dissolve into black ink, from the cap edge upwards. The white stem is smooth and hollow. Its thin ring slides and often drops to the base. The spore print is black. The common ink cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) has a smooth, grey-brown, finely grooved cap with no shaggy scales. It grows in clusters from buried wood. On US lawns, young green-spored parasols (Chlorophyllum molybdites) can look similar. Their gills never turn black.
guide.habitat: Look on lawns, verges, parks, paths, building sites and other disturbed, grassy ground. It often grows in rows or groups. It is common across Europe and North America.
guide.season: It comes mainly in late summer and autumn, a few days after rain. It comes again in spring. On the US Pacific coast it carries on through the mild, wet winter.
guide.picking: Take only young, closed caps that are white all over, with white gills. Take only what you will cook the same day. Avoid busy roads, dumps and polluted ground, because it takes up heavy metals.
guide.kitchen: When you're certain of the identification, cook it within a few hours. Cut away any pink or black part, which turns bitter. Sauté it in butter, or add it to soups and omelettes. It is mild and delicate. It is not known to react with alcohol. But the common ink cap does, even with drinks taken days before or after the meal. If you are unsure which ink cap you have, do not eat it.
guide.keeps: It does not keep. Within a day it turns to ink, even in the fridge. Cook it straight away. Cooked, it keeps a day or two in the fridge, or you can freeze it.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature and Missouri Department of Conservation. Alcohol reaction: First Nature. Season: GBIF records.

giant_puffball.name: Giant Puffball
giant_puffball.description: A smooth white ball, football-sized or bigger, in meadows and pastures, with firm white flesh like fresh mozzarella
giant_puffball.howTo: Look in meadows, pastures, parks and woodland edges from late summer to autumn, often where nettles grow. Cut every one in half from top to bottom: it must be pure white inside, with no trace of a cap or stem

guide.identify: The giant puffball is a smooth white ball, often 20 to 50 cm across. It has a thin, leathery skin and no stem. A cord-like root joins it to the ground. Cut every one in half from top to bottom. The inside must be firm and pure white throughout, like fresh mozzarella. Any outline of a cap, gills or stem can mean a young Amanita still in its egg. That can be deadly. A thick, scaly, yellowish skin and a dark, purple-black inside mean an earthball (Scleroderma), which is poisonous. Yellow, olive or brown flesh means the spores are ripening. Then it is no longer edible.
guide.habitat: Look in meadows, pastures, parks, gardens, hedgerows and woodland edges on rich ground. It often grows among nettles, and often in the same place every year. It is widespread in Europe and the eastern US. In the dry interior West the similar western giant puffball (Calvatia booniana) grows in sagebrush and open grassland.
guide.season: It grows from summer to autumn. In Europe that is mainly July to October. In the eastern US it is late summer to early autumn. It swells fast after warm, heavy rain.
guide.picking: Cut it at the base and take only firm ones that are white inside. One usually feeds several people. Leave old, yellowing ones to spread their spores. Avoid roadsides and lawns treated with chemicals.
guide.kitchen: When you're sure of it, peel off the skin, which can be hard to digest. Then cook it. Fry thick slices in butter, or bread them first. It tastes mild and takes up other flavours. Try a small amount the first time.
guide.keeps: Keep it in the fridge and eat it within two days. Throw it away once the flesh turns yellow. Fried slices freeze well.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Missouri Department of Conservation and First Nature. Storage: ANSES. Season: GBIF records.

matsutake.name: Matsutake
matsutake.description: A firm white-and-brown mushroom with a spicy, cinnamon-like smell, prized above all others in Japan
matsutake.howTo: Look in dry, sandy pine heaths from August in the Nordics, and under conifers and tanoak from September to November in the western US. Never rake the ground. It is red-listed in Sweden and Norway, where logging, not picking, is the threat; US national forests require a permit

guide.identify: Matsutake is a firm, heavy mushroom. The cap is 6 to 20 cm across, white with brown fibres and scales. In Europe and Asia it is browner. When young, the cap edge is rolled in. The gills are crowded, white to cream and attached to the stem. A thick white veil leaves a flaring ring. Below the ring, brown scales sheathe the stem. The solid stem narrows towards the base, with no bulb, sac or cup. The smell is strong and spicy, like cinnamon with a note of dirty socks. Without that smell it is not a matsutake. But the smell alone is no proof. Smith's amanita (Amanita smithiana) and the destroying angels are white too. These are Amanita virosa in Europe, A. bisporigera in the East and A. ocreata in the West. They have a bulb, sac or warty rings at the very base. Their ring is ragged or skirt-like, and they have no spicy smell. They destroy the kidneys or liver.
guide.habitat: It lives with trees on poor, well-drained soil. In Europe you find it mainly in Finland, Sweden and Norway. There it grows in dry, lichen-rich pine heaths on sand or gravel. In western North America it grows under pines, Douglas fir, hemlock, firs and tanoak, often on sandy or pumice soil. In the East, look under jack pine, red pine and eastern hemlock, in the north and the Appalachians.
guide.season: In the Nordic countries it comes from August to October. It follows late-summer rain, once the nights turn cool. In North America the season runs from September to November. On the Pacific coast it goes on into December.
guide.picking: Rock it gently out of the ground. Then fill the hole and put back the moss and needles. Never rake or dig, because that damages the fungus and future crops. Matsutake is listed as Vulnerable worldwide (IUCN). It is red-listed in Sweden and Norway, where the threat is the loss of old pine forest, not picking. US national forests set their own matsutake permits and limits, so check with the ranger district.
guide.kitchen: Wait until you have identified it with certainty. Then wipe it clean and trim the stem base, but don't wash it. Never eat it raw. Cook it gently and briefly to keep the aroma. Slice and grill it, cook it with rice or add it to a clear broth. It is firm and chewy, with a spicy, pine-like scent.
guide.keeps: Wrap it in paper and keep it in the fridge. Use it within a few days, before the smell fades.
guide.source: Identification: UBC Beaty Biodiversity Museum and MushroomExpert.com. Look-alikes: North American Mycological Association poisoning reports. Status: IUCN Red List. Picking rules: US Forest Service. Season: GBIF records.

ramps.name: Ramps
ramps.description: America's wild garlic: broad, smooth green leaves on purplish stems that smell strongly of onion and garlic
ramps.howTo: Look in rich, moist hardwood forest in the eastern US from March to May, before the trees leaf out. Take one leaf per plant and leave the bulb; some parks ban picking, and Quebec bans selling them

guide.identify: Ramps grow two or three broad, smooth, flat leaves straight from a small bulb in the ground. Each leaf has its own stalk, often purplish-red near the base. The leaves wither by early summer. After that, a leafless stalk carries a rounded cluster of small white flowers. Crush a leaf. Ramps smell strongly of onion and garlic, and their deadly look-alikes do not. But the smell stays on your fingers, so after the first few leaves the test proves nothing. Check every plant by its leaves and stalks too. False hellebore has pleated leaves set along an upright stem and grows in wet ground. Lily of the valley has two or three leaves wrapped around one another at the base. Autumn crocus, a garden escape, has stalkless leaves in a tuft. Appalachian bunchflower (Melanthium parviflorum) has similar basal leaves but no onion smell.
guide.habitat: Ramps grow in rich, moist deciduous forest with deep leaf litter. Look on shaded slopes and in stream bottoms. They range from Quebec and New England through the Appalachians to Georgia, and west to Minnesota.
guide.season: The leaves come up from March in the southern Appalachians. Further north they appear in April and May. You get them in the few weeks before the trees leaf out. By late May or June they yellow and die back.
guide.picking: Take one leaf per plant, cut with a knife, and leave the bulb. Digging it up kills the plant. It needs at least five years from seed to reach picking size. Ramps have declined in parts of their range. Great Smoky Mountains National Park bans picking. Some national forests limit it and ban selling. Quebec lists ramps as vulnerable and bans their sale. Check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Once you've identified them with certainty, you'll find the leaves taste of strong garlic and onion. Use a few raw, or wilt them briefly into eggs, potatoes, pasta and butter.
guide.keeps: The leaves keep a few days in the fridge, wrapped in a damp cloth. Chopped leaves, ramp butter and pesto all freeze well.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and picking: NC State Extension and United Plant Savers. Look-alikes: Vermont Department of Health. Rules: National Park Service, USDA Forest Service and Quebec's environment ministry. Season: GBIF records.

fiddleheads.name: Fiddleheads
fiddleheads.description: The tightly coiled young fronds of the ostrich fern: smooth, bright green, with brown papery scales
fiddleheads.howTo: Look on river floodplains and in moist woods from late April to May, while the fronds are still coiled. Always boil them before eating, and take no more than half the fiddleheads of a clump

guide.identify: Only the ostrich fern is picked. It grows in clumps, called crowns, of about three to twelve fiddleheads. These are tight green coils about 2.5 cm across. The stem is smooth, with a deep U-shaped groove on its inner side. Thin brown papery scales cover them and rub off. Last year's fertile fronds often still stand in the clump. They are dark brown, stiff and shaped like feathers. Bracken is carcinogenic. It comes up singly from creeping stems under the ground. Its stem is fuzzy and round, it has no papery scales and its top branches in three. Other ferns, such as cinnamon fern, have woolly fiddleheads and are not recommended.
guide.habitat: It grows on shaded river floodplains and sandbars and in rich, moist woods, often under maple and ash. In the US it is common in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes. It reaches south to Pennsylvania and west to the Dakotas. In the West it is rare outside Alaska. In Europe it grows along streams in the north and centre.
guide.season: Fiddleheads come up in spring as the ground warms after snowmelt and floods. In southern Maine that means late April. In the far north it is mid to late May, and in places into early June. Pick them while they are 5 to 15 cm tall and tightly coiled. Within days they unroll and are past eating.
guide.picking: Only pick from healthy clumps with at least four fiddleheads. Take no more than half, and don't come back that season. Picking them all weakens or kills the fern. Ask the landowner first. In Germany the wild ostrich fern is protected by law, so leave it there.
guide.kitchen: Never eat fiddleheads raw or lightly cooked. They have caused outbreaks of food poisoning, with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and cramps, investigated by the US CDC. Make sure of your identification first. Rub off the brown scales and wash them in several changes of cold water. Then boil them in small batches in plenty of salted water for 15 minutes. Or steam them for 10 to 12 minutes. Throw the water away. Only then sauté them or add them to dishes. They taste of asparagus and green beans.
guide.keeps: Keep them in the fridge and use them within a week. To freeze them, blanch small batches for 2 minutes. Cool them in ice water, drain them and freeze them. They still need the full 15 minutes of boiling before you eat them.
guide.source: Identification, season, picking and cooking: University of Maine Cooperative Extension. Food poisoning: US CDC. US range: Penn State Extension. Protection in Germany: Federal Species Protection Ordinance (BArtSchV).

cloudberry.name: Cloudberry
cloudberry.description: An amber-orange berry of northern bogs, like a soft raspberry, prized across the Nordic countries
cloudberry.howTo: Look on open bogs and wet heath in Fennoscandia in July and August, when the berries turn from hard red to soft amber-yellow. A frost at flowering time can ruin a year's crop

guide.identify: Cloudberry is a low herb, not a shrub, about a hand high. It rises from creeping stems under the ground. Each upright shoot carries one to three round, wrinkled leaves with five to seven shallow lobes. It has a single white flower. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, so only some shoots bear fruit. The berry looks like a raspberry made of a few large drupelets. It is hard and red at first. When ripe it turns soft and amber-orange.
guide.habitat: It grows on open bogs, wet heath, mires and tundra, often among sphagnum moss and dwarf birch. It is common in Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Baltic states and Russia. You also find it on high moorland in Scotland and northern England. In Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic it survives only in a few bogs, as a relic of the Ice Age. There it is protected or listed as endangered.
guide.season: It flowers in June. The berries ripen from mid-July in the south of Scandinavia and the Baltic. In the far north and in the mountains they ripen in August. A frost at flowering time can ruin a year's crop.
guide.picking: Only pick soft, amber berries that come off easily. Hard red ones are not ripe. Everyman's right lets anyone pick them in Sweden, Finland and Norway. In Nordland, Troms and Finnmark, though, the landowner may ban picking on productive cloudberry bogs. The ban is announced by signs or in a newspaper. You may then still eat berries on the spot. On public land in Finnmark, only residents may pick them to sell. Nature reserves can have their own rules. In central Europe the plant must be left alone. Check the local rules before you go.
guide.kitchen: Be sure of what you have first. Then eat them fresh with cream or on waffles, or cook them into jam. In Finland the jam goes with warm squeaky cheese (leipäjuusto). In Sweden it goes over ice cream. The taste is tart and aromatic.
guide.keeps: Ripe berries keep only a day or two in the fridge. They freeze well. Their natural benzoic acid helps the jam keep.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: University of Alberta and Minnesota Wildflowers. Picking rules: Norwegian Environment Agency and Swedish Environmental Protection Agency. Status in central Europe: Czech and German red lists.

huckleberry.name: Huckleberry
huckleberry.description: A purple-black mountain berry of the US Northwest, sweeter and tarter than a blueberry
huckleberry.howTo: Look on subalpine slopes and old burns at 1,000–2,000 m in Montana, Idaho and the Cascades from July to September. Huckleberry patches are bear country: make noise and carry bear spray

guide.identify: Huckleberry is a deciduous shrub, usually waist to shoulder high. Its young twigs are slightly angled and yellow-green. The leaves are thin and oval, with a pointed tip and finely toothed edges. In early summer creamy-pink, urn-shaped flowers hang singly from the leaf axils. Each gives one purple to reddish-black berry, usually without a pale bloom. At its tip sits a small ring shaped like a crown. Berries you should not eat grow in the same forests, but they grow differently. Twinberry honeysuckle (Lonicera involucrata) has black berries in pairs inside red bracts. Baneberry (Actaea rubra) is a soft herb with clustered red or white berries.
guide.habitat: Look in mountain conifer forests, on open subalpine slopes and on old burns. The shrubs fruit best in sun. Its range runs from British Columbia south through the Cascades and the Northern Rockies to California. That takes in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. Outlying stands reach east to the Black Hills and the upper Great Lakes. In the eastern US the name huckleberry usually means Gaylussacia. That is a different shrub, whose berries hold ten small, hard seeds.
guide.season: The berries ripen from July at lower elevations to September higher up. On each bush they ripen a few at a time. A late frost at flowering can cut the crop.
guide.picking: Pick by hand, berry by berry, without breaking branches. On US national forests, picking for your own use is often allowed. Sometimes you need a free permit, and there are daily and season limits. Commercial picking needs a permit or is closed. Some fields are reserved for tribes, such as part of the Sawtooth Berry Fields in Washington. Check the forest's rules. Huckleberry patches are bear country, so make noise and carry bear spray.
guide.kitchen: Once you've identified them with certainty, eat them raw or cook them. They go into pies, jam, syrup and pancakes and into sauces for game. They taste more intense than cultivated blueberries, sweet with a tart edge. Rinse them just before use.
guide.keeps: Unwashed and spread out, they keep a few days in the fridge. Freeze them on a tray, then bag them.
guide.source: Identification and range: USDA Forest Service (Fire Effects Information System) and University of British Columbia. Picking rules: Gifford Pinchot National Forest. Look-alikes: US National Park Service.

pawpaw.name: Pawpaw
pawpaw.description: North America's largest native fruit: green and mango-shaped, with custardy flesh that tastes of banana and mango
pawpaw.howTo: Look in the understory of river-bottom forests in the eastern US from late August to October, when the fruit softens and drops. Eat only the flesh: the skin and seeds are poisonous

guide.identify: Pawpaw is a small understory tree. It often forms patches from root suckers. The leaves are large and drooping, and widest beyond the middle. Crushed, they smell of green pepper. In spring, deep maroon flowers with six petals open before the leaves. The fruit is oblong and green to yellow-green. It grows singly or in clusters of two to nine. Inside, soft yellow, custard-like flesh surrounds two rows of large, flat brown seeds.
guide.habitat: Pawpaw grows in moist, rich woods on river floodplains, stream banks and shady lower slopes. It is native across the eastern US, from northern Florida to the Great Lakes and southern Ontario. Westwards it reaches eastern Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. It does not grow wild in the western US.
guide.season: The fruit ripens from late August in the south and in September and October in the north. A tree's crop ripens over one to two weeks. Ripe fruit drops to the ground.
guide.picking: A ripe fruit gives slightly when you squeeze it gently, like a peach. It also smells strongly fruity. Skin colour is not a reliable sign. Gather fresh windfalls or shake the trunk gently. In season, check every day or two. Handle the fruit carefully, as it bruises easily.
guide.kitchen: When you're certain of the tree, eat only the flesh. Cut the fruit in half lengthwise and scoop the flesh away from the skin and seeds. Never eat or chew the skin or seeds. The flesh tastes of banana and mango. It can replace banana in breads, ice cream and puddings. Wild fruit can have a bitter aftertaste. Some people react with vomiting or an allergic reaction, so try a small amount first. Medical sources also advise against eating it in large amounts over long periods. The flesh contains annonacin, a compound that was toxic to nerve cells in laboratory studies.
guide.keeps: Ripe fruit lasts only a few days at room temperature and about a week in the fridge. Fruit picked just before it is fully ripe keeps up to three weeks in the fridge. Then it finishes ripening at room temperature. The scooped flesh freezes for up to a year.
guide.source: Identification and range: University of Kentucky Center for Crop Diversification. Ripeness, preparation and keeping: Purdue Extension. Reactions: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.

rose_hips.name: Rose Hips
rose_hips.description: The red autumn fruits of wild roses, rich in vitamin C and full of seeds wrapped in itchy hairs
rose_hips.howTo: Look on hedgerows, scrub and woodland edges from late August to November; they are softest after the first frosts. Remove the seeds and hairs, which irritate the mouth and gut

guide.identify: Dog rose is a shrub with long arching stems and strongly hooked prickles. Its leaves have 5 to 7 toothed leaflets. The hips are oval, smooth and glossy scarlet, 1 to 2 cm long. When ripe they have no sepals left on them. Inside, hard seeds sit in fine, irritant hairs. Black bryony, white bryony and bittersweet grow in the same hedges. They hang shiny red, poisonous berries in bunches, on climbing stems without prickles. A rose hip grows on a prickly rose stem and is full of hairy seeds.
guide.habitat: Dog rose grows in hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges and rough grassland across Europe. You find it from the lowlands into the mountains. In the US dog rose grows wild in places. There you can use the hips of native wild roses and of rugosa rose the same way.
guide.season: Hips ripen from September to November. Many stay on the bush into winter. Frost makes them softer and sweeter. But the longer they hang, the less vitamin C they hold.
guide.picking: Pick firm, fully coloured hips that give a little when pressed. Take a few from each bush and leave plenty for birds. Wear gloves, and avoid roadsides and sprayed hedges.
guide.kitchen: Once you're certain of them, eat only the pulp. The seeds and their hairs irritate the mouth, gut and skin. Cut off the stalk and tip, halve the hips and scrape out every seed and hair. Or simmer them whole and press them through a fine sieve. Then strain the juice again through muslin. Use the pulp for syrup, jelly, jam and tea. It goes well with apple.
guide.keeps: Fresh hips keep about a week in the fridge. They freeze well. Seeded halves dried at no more than 50 °C keep for many months in an airtight jar.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Woodland Trust and The Wildlife Trusts. Season, picking and cooking: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension and Bundeszentrum für Ernährung (BZfE).

sloes.name: Sloes
sloes.description: The small blue-black fruits of the thorny blackthorn, with a dusty bloom and a fiercely sour taste
sloes.howTo: Look on hedgerows and scrubby slopes from September to November; they mellow after the first frosts. Don't crush the stones, and watch for shiny black look-alikes such as buckthorn and deadly nightshade

guide.identify: Sloes grow on blackthorn. It is a dense, woody shrub with dark bark, and its side twigs end in sharp thorns. The white blossom opens in March and April, before the leaves. The fruit is round and about 1 cm across. It is blue-black with a dusty bloom that rubs off. Sloes grow singly or in pairs along the twigs. Inside, green and very astringent flesh surrounds one stone. Buckthorn has shiny black berries in clusters, with no bloom. Deadly nightshade is a soft, leafy herb, not a thorny shrub. Its shiny black berries grow singly, each sitting in a green star of sepals.
guide.habitat: Blackthorn grows in hedgerows, scrub and woodland edges and on sunny, stony slopes. It often forms thickets that spread by suckers. You find it across most of Europe, north and south, from the lowlands into the hills.
guide.season: Sloes ripen from September to November. They are ready when they are dark and soft enough to squash between your fingers. People traditionally pick them after the first frost. Frost splits the skins and softens the fruit, so the juice runs out. You can pick them earlier and freeze them overnight, which does the same.
guide.picking: Wear gloves, because the thorns are long and sharp. Pick from several bushes and leave plenty for birds. Avoid roadside hedges and sprayed field edges.
guide.kitchen: Make sure they're sloes first. They are too sour and astringent to eat raw. But they make sloe gin and other liqueurs, such as Spanish pacharán in anise spirit. They also make a jelly with apples. For gin, prick or freeze them, then cover them with sugar and gin. Leave them a few months in a dark place, shaking now and then, and strain. Never crush or crack the stones. The kernels contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide.
guide.keeps: Fresh sloes keep a few days in the fridge. Frozen in sealed bags they keep for months. They go straight from the freezer into the jar.
guide.source: Identification, habitat and the frost tradition: Woodland Trust. Stones: USDA Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases.

sea_buckthorn.name: Sea Buckthorn
sea_buckthorn.description: Bright orange berries packed along thorny, silver-leaved branches: sour and rich in vitamin C
sea_buckthorn.howTo: Look on coastal dunes and gravelly riverbanks from August to October. Wear gloves against the thorns, and check the rules: picking is often forbidden in dune reserves

guide.identify: Sea buckthorn is a thorny, much-branched shrub that forms thickets. Its narrow, willow-like leaves are covered in silvery scales, above all underneath. Male and female flowers grow on separate bushes, so only female bushes fruit. The berries are round and bright orange, 6 to 8 mm across. They sit packed tightly along the twigs on very short stalks. They are juicy and very sour, and they burst at a touch. Rowan and firethorn also have orange berries. But they carry them in stalked bunches among green leaves.
guide.habitat: It needs full sun and open sand or gravel. Look on the coastal dunes of the North Sea, the Baltic and eastern England. It also grows on dry gravel banks and terraces of rivers in the Alps and their foothills. In southern Europe it is mostly a plant of mountain river gravels, in the Alps and the Pyrenees. It is also planted on embankments and roadsides.
guide.season: The berries ripen from August into October. They are most aromatic early in ripening. They hang on into winter, but overripe berries taste rancid.
guide.picking: Wild stands often grow in dune and riverside nature reserves, where picking is forbidden. Check the local rules first. Never cut branches from wild bushes. Wear gloves. Hold a bowl under the twig as you pick, because the berries burst. Leave plenty for wintering thrushes.
guide.kitchen: If you're certain of the identification, you can eat the berries raw. But they are very sour, slightly bitter and they stain. Most people cook them briefly with a little water and honey or sugar. Then they strain them for juice, syrup, jelly or purée. Apple or apricot softens the sharpness. The purée suits yoghurt, muesli, ice cream and soups.
guide.keeps: Fresh berries spoil quickly. Freeze them, or freeze the juice in portions. You can dry the pulp left after pressing for tea.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: The Wildlife Trusts and the European Environment Agency (EUNIS). Season, cooking and keeping: Bundeszentrum für Ernährung (BZfE).

boletus.name: Boletus (porcini & bay bolete)
boletus.description: Porcini and the bay bolete in one score: porcini, pine, bronze and summer boletes, the bay bolete in Europe and the North American kings
boletus.howTo: Each place shows the best of their scores; look in beech, oak, chestnut, pine and spruce woods two to four weeks after a soaking rain

guide.identify: This group brings together several boletes. In Europe there are the porcini (Boletus edulis) and the pine, bronze and summer boletes. North America adds the eastern king bolete and the Rocky Mountain king. The bay bolete (Imleria badia) belongs here too. The porcini and kings have white pores when young, a net on the stem and white flesh that does not turn blue. The bay bolete has yellow pores that bruise blue-green and a streaky stem without a net. The cap tells them apart. It is brown and greasy on the porcino, wine-red on the pine bolete and near-black and velvety on the bronze bolete. The summer bolete's cap is pale and cracked, and the eastern king's is tan to lilac-brown. The Rocky Mountain king has a brick-red cap and the bay bolete a chestnut, tacky one. Red or orange pores mean a toxic bolete, such as the devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas). Pink pores and a dark stem net mean the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus).
guide.habitat: All of them live with trees. Porcini grow with conifers, beech and oak. The pine bolete grows with pine and spruce. The bronze and summer boletes like oak and chestnut in warm woods. The bay bolete grows with conifers on acid sand. The eastern king grows in eastern US oak woods, and the Rocky Mountain king under high spruce.
guide.season: Between them they run from May to the first frosts. The summer bolete starts in May. At the other end, the bay bolete peaks in October and November. Porcini fruit mainly from August to October. Flushes follow a soaking rain by two to three weeks.
guide.picking: Only pick what you can name with certainty, and keep each kind apart in your basket. Germany allows porcini only in small amounts for your own use and protects the bronze bolete. Italy and Spain often require permits.
guide.kitchen: Identify each one with certainty first. Then brush them all, slice them to check for maggots and cook them through. The bay bolete gathers radioactive caesium. In parts of Bavaria and Austria, eat it only now and then.
guide.keeps: They all dry well in thin slices.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: Regione Piemonte, First Nature and MushroomExpert. Season: GBIF records. Rules: BArtSchV (Germany). Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS).

cantharellus.name: Chanterelles (all)
cantharellus.description: Every chanterelle in one score: the golden chanterelles, the black trumpet and the winter chanterelle, and in North America the smooth and Pacific chanterelles
cantharellus.howTo: Each place shows the best of their scores; golden chanterelles on mossy slopes under oak, beech and conifers after warm rain, black trumpets in damp leaf litter under broadleaves, winter chanterelles on wet moss under conifers late in the season

guide.identify: This group holds five species. They are the golden chanterelle, the smooth and Pacific chanterelles of North America, the black trumpet and the winter chanterelle. The last two belong to the close genus Craterellus. All of them have blunt, forking ridges or a nearly smooth underside running down the stem. They never have thin, blade-like gills. The golden, smooth and Pacific chanterelles are yellow to orange and fleshy, with a solid stem. The winter chanterelle is small, with a brown cap and a hollow yellow stem. The black trumpet is a thin, hollow, grey-black horn. Each has its own dangerous look-alike. For the yellow ones it is the jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus), with true gills and clusters on wood. Among winter chanterelles it is the deadly webcap (Cortinarius rubellus), with rusty-brown gills.
guide.habitat: All of them live with tree roots. The golden chanterelle grows under broadleaves and conifers across Europe and North America. The black trumpet likes damp leaf litter, mainly under beech and oak. The winter chanterelle grows on wet moss and rotten wood under conifers. The smooth chanterelle belongs to eastern US oak woods. The Pacific chanterelle belongs to the Douglas fir and hemlock forests of the Pacific Northwest.
guide.season: Together they run from early summer to winter. Golden and smooth chanterelles come from early summer, after warm rain. Black trumpets follow from late summer through autumn. Pacific and winter chanterelles run from autumn into winter, until hard frost. In the western US they follow the autumn and winter rains.
guide.picking: Cut or twist them at the base. Leave the small ones and take only what you will eat. In Germany the golden chanterelle is specially protected. You may pick only small amounts there, for your own use. Other countries, regions and US public lands set their own limits or permits, so check the local rules.
guide.kitchen: Identify each mushroom with certainty first. Cook them all well, and never eat them raw. Golden, smooth and Pacific chanterelles are fruity and firm. They are best fried slowly in butter. Black trumpets taste smoky and winter chanterelles earthy. Both are good in sauces and risotto and with eggs. Split trumpets and winter chanterelles lengthwise to rinse out the grit.
guide.keeps: Fresh, they keep a few days in the fridge in paper, not plastic. Black trumpets and winter chanterelles dry very well. Golden chanterelles turn tough when dried. They are better fried and frozen.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature (UK), MushroomExpert.com and MykoWeb (California Fungi). Deadly webcap: Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Protection: German Federal Species Protection Ordinance. Season: GBIF records.

bay_bolete.name: Bay Bolete
bay_bolete.description: A chestnut-brown capped bolete, tacky when wet, with cream to olive-yellow pores that bruise blue-green and a streaky stem without a net
bay_bolete.howTo: Look in moss under pine and spruce, also beech and oak, on acid sandy soil from August to the first frosts; it peaks in October as porcini fade. It gathers more Chernobyl caesium than most mushrooms, so in Bavaria and Austria eat it only now and then

guide.identify: This is a bolete without the porcini's net on the stem. The cap is chestnut brown. It feels like suede when dry and turns sticky when wet. The pores are cream to pale yellow, later olive, and bruise blue-green. The flesh is white to pale yellow and may turn faintly blue when you cut it. The stem is slimmer and streaked brown on a paler background. Red or orange pores rule it out (Rubroboletus satanas, Neoboletus subvelutipes). So do pink pores with a netted stem (Tylopilus felleus). In eastern North America there are two more to know. Boletus sensibilis turns dark blue instantly all over and has a yellow stem. Boletus huronensis is dense and shaped like a porcino, with a yellowish stem.
guide.habitat: It grows with pine and spruce, and also with beech, oak and chestnut. It likes acid, sandy soil and often sits in moss near old stumps. It is common in the lowlands of northern and central Europe. In North America it grows in the north-east, around the Great Lakes and in the Appalachians, under pine and hemlock.
guide.season: In Europe it fruits from August until the first hard frosts. It peaks in October, after the porcini, and runs into December in the south. In north-eastern North America it comes earlier, mainly from July to September.
guide.picking: Twist it out or cut it, and leave the young and the old ones. Check the local rules, as picking is often banned in nature reserves.
guide.kitchen: First make sure of your identification. Wipe the cap and peel it if it is slimy. Remove any soft old tubes and cook it through. Any blue disappears in cooking, and the taste is mild. It gathers more radioactive caesium than most mushrooms. In parts of Bavaria and Austria, eat it only now and then.
guide.keeps: It dries well in thin slices. It also freezes well once cooked.
guide.source: Identification and habitat: First Nature and MushroomExpert. Season: GBIF records. Caesium: German Federal Office for Radiation Protection (BfS) and Bavarian LGL.
